chapterReports.title: 來自我自己的訊息
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At ten past ten on Monday night, my phone showed me a new message. The name above it was Mia Chen. My name. The small picture was also mine: me at the beach, with one eye closed against the sun. I had not sent myself anything. A moment before, I had been trying to learn twelve English words. I knew three. I was bored. Now I could not look away from the screen.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: My mother knocked and came in with warm milk. She asked if I had finished studying. I said almost. When she left, I opened June's old chat. My last message was still there: Is it true? She had never answered. I wrote, Are you okay? Then I erased it. Outside, rain tapped the glass. My phone lit up one more time. This time, there were only three words. You voted too.

chapterReports.title: 紅圍巾
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: I went to school. Of course I did. At sixteen, you can be afraid of something and still be more afraid of missing the thing everyone else will see. I told myself I was going because of the science test. I even carried my science book in my hand, as if the book could prove it. The rain had stopped, but the steps were still wet.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: My phone shook in my hand. Another Later message. See? Now you believe me. The next sentence was longer. At lunch, your name will reach fifty percent. Find the blue door before then. I looked up at the second floor. Every window was closed except one. Behind it, for half a second, I saw a sleeve the same yellow as June's old raincoat.

chapterReports.title: 藍門後面
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: There were eleven blue doors in our school. I learned this by walking past ten wrong ones before lunch. The art room was blue. So was the nurse's room. Even the little cupboard where Mr Han kept the floor brushes had a blue door. Leo followed me with a paper map. “Maybe the message means any blue door,” he said. “That would be very bad writing.”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Leo wanted to tell Ms Lin, our English teacher. I said we needed to understand first. It sounded reasonable. Really, I did not want a teacher asking why someone had sent me that old voice file. We left the notebook where we found it and stepped outside. My screen lit up. Mia: forty-nine percent. Then Sam's name vanished from the vote. In its place appeared a new name. Leo Wu.

chapterReports.title: 一個名字換一個名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Leo stared at his name for a long time. Then he put his phone away and finished the cold bread from breakfast. He tore it into small, even pieces. I knew that habit. When Leo was angry, everything had to be straight. His pencils. His books. The little pieces of bread on his desk. “We need to find Sam,” he said. His voice was very quiet.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: When Sam left, Leo turned to me. “You haven't shown me everything.” I opened the voice file at last. My voice filled the empty hall. June, wait. Give me the phone. Leo listened twice. “That's from the school film folder,” he said. “Only three people had the link.” “You, June, and who?” He looked toward the stage doors. From inside came Kai's voice, testing a microphone.

chapterReports.title: 拿麥克風的男孩
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Kai saw us through the open stage door. “Come help,” he called. “I need two normal people to test the seats.” Leo looked at me. We went in, but we stayed near the door. The hall smelled of warm wood and dust. Paper stars hung above the stage. In three days, parents would sit here and clap while Kai told them what a happy school this was.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: I opened it anyway. The letter was only one line: Ask what happened to the money before you trust the adults. Below it was a photo of an empty cash box. A little piece of white paper lay inside. It was a receipt. I made the picture larger. The date matched the day June left. The name at the bottom was not June's. It was Principal Reed's.

chapterReports.title: 空錢盒
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ms Lin read the messages without once saying that we were being too sensitive. She placed her phone beside mine and asked before taking pictures. When she reached the old voice file, I looked at the clock. Its second hand seemed very loud. “Is that your voice?” she asked. I nodded. “Do you remember what happened around those words?” I remembered. I had worked hard not to.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: At home, I changed my Later password with Leo talking me through the account settings. The future letters stopped. For twenty minutes, I felt in control. Then an email arrived at my school address. No false future date this time. Just a photo. It showed the red notebook open on a desk. On the next page, in my own handwriting, was the vote I had thought nobody could see.

chapterReports.title: 我的字跡
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The words in the photograph were mine, but they were not a vote. I pulled an old exercise book from my shelf and found the page. Six weeks ago, our class had written an opinion for a lesson about online news. I had written, I believe June took the money because the video shows her by the box. I remembered feeling proud of the clear sentence.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: I wanted to tell him I trusted him. I also wanted to ask exactly what he had kept. Both feelings were true, and neither made the other leave. I finally wrote, We check it with Ms Lin. Not alone. He sent back one word: Okay. Before I slept, I checked the Zero page once more. The vote was closed. Under Leo's name was a new title: The Boy Who Saved Everything.

chapterReports.title: 他留下的一切
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Wednesday morning, Leo arrived at Ms Lin's room carrying a small gray drive. He held it with both hands, as if it were hot. I came early too, but he would not look at me. Ms Lin closed the door and put a sign outside saying she was in a meeting. Then she asked Leo what he wanted us to know before we opened anything.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: The recording continued. My own footsteps entered the room. June grabbed the phone. I told her to stop. Then, at the place where the short video ended, June spoke again. “Mia, look at the screen. Please look.” I had not looked. In the recording, I heard myself answer instead. “Just give it back.” Ms Lin stopped the sound gently. Nobody in the room was looking at me now.

chapterReports.title: 剪接之後的那一段
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: I asked to hear the rest. Ms Lin watched my face before she pressed play. In the recording, June said she had sent a copy to herself. Kai asked her to delete it. She said no. There was a loud scrape, then my voice, asking them both to stop. The sound broke for a moment. When it returned, Kai was laughing. “Who will they believe?” he asked.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: On the back was a rough drawing of a giant vote screen. Four faces would appear while the audience chose one. I recognized my school picture, Leo's, Sam's, and June's. Ada touched the corner of the paper. “I saved the messages,” she said. “But there's something else.” She turned her phone toward me. Bell had sent her an instruction for Friday: Make sure Mia comes to school.

chapterReports.title: 兩種不同的警告
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Don't come to school. Make sure Mia comes to school. I wrote both sentences on a clean page. For two days, I had treated every strange message as one voice. Now I drew a line between them. The Later letters wanted me away. Bell wanted me here. One used my old voice to pull me toward June. The other used names and numbers to move people around.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: At nine, Leo sent me a screenshot from the old film list. The computer teacher had found that the broken video was not the only full copy. Another had been sent to the school show laptop. Its file name was simple: Friday. Then a message arrived from June. Before we meet, there is one thing you should know. I sent the letters. But I did not write the first warning.

chapterReports.title: 第一個警告
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Thursday, Sam was waiting by my classroom before the lights came on. He had two dark half circles under his eyes. “June said I could tell you,” he began. “The first warning was mine.” He showed me his own message to her, sent on Monday afternoon. Don't come to school tomorrow. Please. Below it was a photo of the list Bell had given him.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: I took a photo and sent it to Mum. She answered, We will ask for facts. No need to be polite about missing facts. I smiled for the first time that morning. Then Kai appeared at the classroom door. He held a white envelope with my name on it. “Before you go to Reed,” he said, “you should know what he told me to do.”

chapterReports.title: 太乾淨的道歉
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: I did not open Kai's envelope in the hall. We took it to Ms Lin. He came too, walking half a step ahead as if this had been his idea. Inside was a printed message from Mr Reed to the school show team. It said, Please remove the argument from the final film. We want families to see the positive side of our school. Kai watched us read it.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Outside the office, Kai waited by the drinking fountain. “I can make your name disappear from the page,” he said quietly. “You only have to stop.” I looked at him, at the easy offer he had probably made to Sam. “A name for a name?” I asked. He did not answer. My phone buzzed. June was already at the library. For once, I knew exactly where I wanted to go.

chapterReports.title: 四號桌的女孩
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: June was eating a cheese sandwich when I saw her. I had imagined tears, maybe a long silence, maybe her walking away before I could speak. I had not imagined a sandwich. She looked up, covered her mouth to finish chewing, and pointed at the chair across from her. Her hair was shorter. There was a small spot of yellow paint on her left sleeve.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: I wanted to argue. I wanted to hug her. Instead I asked whether she had sent the photo of my handwriting. She nodded. Bell had sent it to her as a threat against me. She had forwarded it without explaining, hoping I would finally understand how easy a cut could be. “I'm sorry for that too,” she said. Then she placed a small memory card between us. “This part isn't a trick.”

chapterReports.title: 鏡頭看見的事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The memory card was a copy of June's own camera files. She had brought it for Ms Lin, not for me to take home. She called her mother and our teacher over. Before anyone opened it, she named the parts she did not want shared. There was a clip of Sam after a difficult phone call. There were private talks between friends. “Those are not the price of proving I didn't steal,” she said.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Ms Lin said the school now had enough to make a clear correction about the money and to begin a full review of the page. She asked whether June wanted to attend Friday's show. June said she did not know. Then she opened one last file. It was not a video. It was a screenshot of Bell's latest message. If you give them the card, the next name is your mother's.

chapterReports.title: 威脅不是投票
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: June's mother read the message without changing her face. Then she moved her chair close to June's. “We are not trading anyone's safety for silence,” she said. Ms Lin asked if the message included an address or a plan to approach them. It did not. They saved the original message and agreed on what to report and who would follow up. Nobody asked June to answer Bell.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: On the way home, Mum drove while I read a new school notice. The first line said, There has been no theft of school show money by June Park. I read it aloud. For six weeks, that sentence had been missing. Now it existed. Under it was a link to a private reporting form. Above it, my phone showed a new alert. Zero was running one final vote. Should Mia tell everyone what she did?

chapterReports.title: 百分之九十九
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: By Thursday evening, ninety-nine percent of Zero wanted me to tell everyone what I had done. At least, that was what the page said. Under the number was a place to leave a comment. The first comment called me brave. The second called me a liar. The third asked for June's full video. I closed the page before I could read the rest.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: When I went back upstairs, June had sent another message. I want the correction where the lie was loudest. Not just in an office email. Below it was a voice file. I hesitated before opening it. This time it was her voice, whole and steady. “My name is June Park,” she said. “You have seen twelve seconds of me. That is not the same as knowing what happened.”

chapterReports.title: 另一隻手
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada came to my house that night with her father. Mum made tea while the two adults spoke in the kitchen. We sat at the dining table, where the light was much too bright for secrets. Ada brought her laptop, but she did not open it immediately. She placed both hands flat on the table. “I helped make the first page,” she said. “Before it was called Zero.”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: an update to the families directly involved. Kai and his parent had agreed to provide the account records. The school would check who posted what instead of treating every message as one person's work. At the bottom was a note about Friday: June's statement could be played before the show, if she wanted. Then June called me. “There's a condition,” she said. “No vote afterward.”

chapterReports.title: 後面不准接投票
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: June said the school wanted to end her recording with a question on the screen: What have we learned? Under it, students would choose from three answers. The idea had probably seemed helpful in a meeting. To June, it was another box asking people to press something after looking at her life. “I don't want my worst week turned into a lesson with points,” she said.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Before bed, I recorded my own statement. I did not use music. I did not cut out the place where my voice shook. When I finished, I listened once and sent the text for a fact check. A message arrived from Kai. He wanted to talk before Friday's show. Below that, he wrote something I did not expect. I know where the numbers came from. They were never what you thought.

chapterReports.title: 數字機器
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday morning, Kai met us in the counselor's room with his father. Ms Lin and my mother were there too. I had not agreed to meet him alone. His school shirt was clean, but one button sat in the wrong hole. For the first time, he looked like someone who had dressed too quickly, not someone ready for a stage. He placed a printed account record on the table.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t the wall. “I believed the number,” he said. “Even after I knew the code could be wrong.” I had too. We stood there until the first bell rang. This time nothing fell from a window. Then Ms Lin hurried toward us, holding her phone. The sound system had failed during practice. June's recording could not be played through the hall speakers. The show would start in twenty minutes.

chapterReports.title: 二十分鐘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: For one terrible moment, I thought the school would use the broken speakers as a reason to skip the correction. Mr Reed looked at the silent hall, then at the printed program in his hand. “We can send another email,” he began. Ms Lin shook her head. “The notice and June's chosen statement are part of today's program. We need an accessible way to share them.”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: walked to the front microphone. The room settled. A few phones were still raised, and a teacher reminded everyone that students had not agreed to be filmed. The principal looked at his paper, then lowered it. “Before we begin the show,” he said, “we need to correct something our school should have corrected six weeks ago.” The hall became so quiet I could hear the curtain move.

chapterReports.title: 十二秒不是一個人
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mr Reed said June had not stolen the school show money. He explained the bill for the stage light and the date the office had checked it. He said the short video had left out important context. Then he said the sentence I had been waiting for. “We knew the money had been properly spent, and we failed to correct the public claim. That failure caused harm.”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: For a moment, nothing happened. The quiet was not a punishment. It was simply space where a vote might once have been. I walked behind the curtain, and Leo handed me water without saying I had done well. On the table beside it lay a folded paper bird. One wing was badly bent. Inside, in June's small handwriting, were four words. Thank you for stopping there.

chapterReports.title: 安靜之後
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The show went on. A first-year student played the piano on a real piano, which did not need the broken sound system. Two dancers missed the same step and laughed without looking ashamed. The hall slowly became an ordinary hall again. I was glad. June's morning did not have to swallow everyone else's. She had left with her mother before the first song ended, exactly as she had chosen.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: That afternoon, a student I barely knew stopped at my desk. “I shared the old June video,” he said. “Where should I put the correction?” I showed him the link and asked him to share it in the same groups. He wrote it down. One person. No rising bar. No loud success. On Monday, I would have thought it was too small to matter. On Friday, I made room for it.

chapterReports.title: 需要更久的事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Two weeks passed. The correction stayed at the top of the school page. It was also sent to the class groups through teachers, not left for students to discover by chance. Some old clips remained on private phones. The school could ask people to remove them, but it could not promise that every copy had vanished. I liked the honest limit more than a bright promise nobody could keep.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: That night, Later sent me an automatic email. My original class letter from last year was ready to open. I nearly deleted it. Then I remembered that the site was only a site. Someone had used it to scare me; it did not own every future message. I clicked the letter. Dear Future Mia, it began, please stop losing your keys. Under that was a sentence I had forgotten writing.

chapterReports.title: 我真正寫下的信
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: If June asks you to be in another film, say yes before you get scared. That was the forgotten sentence. Below it, my younger self had added three terrible drawings: a key, a camera, and a bird that looked like a potato. I remembered writing the letter beside June in the computer room. She had laughed at the bird until the teacher asked us to separate our chairs.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: for different buses. June's came first. At the door, she turned and said, “We're not back where we were.” “I know.” “That might be okay.” She got on before I could turn that into a promise. I watched the bus leave, then opened my phone. I started a new Later letter to myself. I did not write a warning. I wrote a date one month away and a question I could answer only by living.

chapterReports.title: 明天，來吧
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: One month later, my phone lit up at ten past ten. The name above the message was Mia Chen. My name. The small picture was still the beach photo with one eye closed. For a moment, my heart moved faster. Then I read the first line of the letter I had really written. Did you listen when the answer was not the one you wanted?
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: wants another short film. Are you free tomorrow? I smiled at the screen. Yes, I wrote. What is it about? Her answer came quickly. A girl keeps getting messages from herself. I stared, then another line appeared. I'm joking. It's about a cat that won't leave a box. Bring a light. Outside, rain touched the glass. I put my phone beside my book and learned one more word before bed.

chapterReports.title: 凌晨六點十分
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At 6:10 a.m., the old warning bell rang above the locked River House. Mia Lin stopped so quickly that a box of breakfast food almost fell from her arms. There had been no rain for days. Why did the bell sound as if the river were rising? The street was empty. Beside Mia, Ruby Chen held a cake in one hand and a bag of fruit in the other. “Did you hear that?” Ruby asked. “Everyone heard that,” Mia s
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Mia had seen was still there, and a small drop of water moved slowly across the ground. “Water has been here recently,” he said. “That much is real.” They did not touch the door. Instead, Mia wrote the date, the time, and what each friend had noticed. As they turned to leave, something knocked once from inside the empty house. It was not the bell. It came from below the floor.

chapterReports.title: 乾天的水聲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the next sunny morning, Leo brought a tool box to the River House, but he did not enter the building. Officer Su had asked everyone to keep out until the town checked the old floor. Leo stood beside the outside power box and showed Mia two wires that were no longer connected. “There is no power going to the bell,” he said. “That means someone pulled the rope, or something else moved it.” Ruby h
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: k here. The picture moves from six ten and two seconds to six ten and nineteen seconds.” Ruby checked it herself. Seventeen seconds were missing. The group stared at the phone, and the friendly morning seemed less friendly. Mia wrote three questions beneath the drawing of the river: What made the water rise? What made the bell ring? What happened during those seventeen seconds?

chapterReports.title: 橋下的白線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next day, Mia began to follow the road from River House toward the old bridge. She had heard about a white line on the ground from a street worker, but she did not know where it started. Jay came in shoes that were too large for him. Ruby carried her camera, and Leo brought a map. They passed the station, then turned toward the beach. A bird rose from the river wall as they walked near it. Far
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: with a light and walked to the locked gate. The night air was still. He did not seem to see Mia at the corner of the street. For a moment she thought of calling to him. Then she saw him bend down and look at the same white line they had found. He knew exactly where it was. Mia took one step forward, then stopped. Why had her father never told her about the path under the road?

chapterReports.title: 便宜的承諾
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday the town held a meeting in the square. A tall board stood beside a small stage, with a drawing of the new factory and a new play area. Mr. Han, the factory manager, said the company could give the town more jobs and a health service room. “The old house is beautiful,” he said, “but the new plan will help living people.” A worker near Mia clapped. A boy beside him called out, “My father n
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ay safe.” Leo gave a small smile. “Then we need more than a photo.” They watched the workers put the board inside. The cheap promise of a new square looked good on paper, but no one had explained where the water would go. At the office door, a notice said that only written records could change the sale decision. They had twenty days, and the paper they needed was still missing.

chapterReports.title: 埋在花圃裡
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Although the meeting had been hard, Grandma Chen asked the children to help with a small race along the river on Saturday. During the event, at least one adult would stand by each crossing. Money from the event would pay for safe paths and fresh plants near the old house. Jay wanted to win the short race, but his real job was to put signs beside the road. He had also made paper snow for a school p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: blue date. His face changed. “Please put it away,” he said. “And promise me you will stay out of the old water way.” “I already promised that,” Mia replied. “But why is that date on the map?” Her father took his plate to the kitchen and stood with his back to her. “Because it was the day I learned that a deal on paper can be very different from real life.” He said nothing more.

chapterReports.title: 叔叔的盒子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mia's uncle asked her to bring old photographs to a family friend downriver. They would travel by boat, then drive the last part of the way. “We have to arrive before lunch,” he told her. “The river can be slow on weekends.” Mia brought the small metal box, hoping he might know the mark drawn on it. On the pier a lion smiled down from a painted shop sign. Inside, the shop sold coffee and sandwiche
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: she asked. Her uncle gave her a sad smile. “You should ask him. But first ask why the bell was tested on a day with no rain. That question has a better answer.” Mia wrote it down. She had another sign now, and this one was on paper. As the boat turned toward the River House, she saw that the old bell had not moved all morning. That silence felt almost as strange as its ringing.

chapterReports.title: 停住的鐘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The clock in River House had stopped at six ten. Mia saw it through the window when Officer Su opened the outside yard for a short visit. No one was allowed into the old building. “I believe someone wants us to remember that time,” Mia said. Leo stood close beside her. “A stopped clock may be an error, not a message.” Jay laughed at the idea of a secret clock, but stopped when he saw Mia's face. H
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: id. “And it always comes from the same side.” They walked around the safe outer yard, watching the gate beyond the fence. The sound seemed to come from below the north wall. Mia wrote this in her notebook, then turned to Leo. “If the clock is only a clock, why does it show the exact time the bell first rang?” Leo looked toward the house. “That,” he said, “is a better question.”

chapterReports.title: 鬼影影片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ruby posted a new video on Sunday night. In it a white shape seemed to fly behind a broken window at River House. She added the words GHOST AT THE RIVER and sent it to her school group. By morning everyone was talking about it. A girl in a red dress said her brother had seen the same ghost from the park. A boy from the baseball team said the house was dangerous. Ruby liked the sudden attention, bu
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ked. “Because we were afraid of the wrong thing,” Mia said. “We have to look behind every picture.” Officer Su came by and told them they had done a good thing by correcting the film. Then she pointed to the old door. “No one has been allowed inside,” she said. As if to answer her, three quick knocks came from behind the locked door. Every person turned toward it. No one moved.

chapterReports.title: 湖邊的舊照片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Grandma Chen took the friends to the lake on the next holiday. A little festival was held there every year, and she kept a box of cards from its early days. “You want to know the past,” she told Mia. “Then visit the people who remember it.” At a food stand, an old woman was serving rice and banana cakes. She knew Grandma Chen and gave the children a warm welcome. “Are you ready for a long story?”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nt her a message: Grandma says the card is important, but please don't be angry with your dad yet. Mia read it twice. She wanted to treat her father fairly; she also wanted him to stop hiding things. The card lay beside the receipt on her desk. Under her father's name there was a small blue mark, the same shape as the one on the old box. Mia turned on her lamp and looked again.

chapterReports.title: 被裁掉的一半
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Monday a picture from twelve years ago appeared online. It showed Mr. Lin near the north gate at night. He was holding a key, and a large metal door was behind him. Someone had written, “This is the man who closed the gate.” Mia saw it between classes and felt a hard hit in her chest. For half a minute she could not move. She knew her father had worked at the gate, but she had never seen him li
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: coat. “There was someone next to your dad,” Ruby wrote. Mia looked at the two pictures together. The old picture had not solved anything. It had only shown how much she still could not see. She wrote one sentence in her notebook: I must not call a half picture a whole story. Then a second message arrived. It was from her father: “Tomorrow, I will take you to the town records.”

chapterReports.title: 藍色的記號
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Officer Su met Mia, her father, and the others at the town office. She explained that some old records could be read by the public, but a worker had to bring the books from storage. The secretary, a quiet woman named Ms. Kao, placed a blue folder on the table. “These are the maps we can show you today,” she said. Mia opened the first sheet carefully. It was a map of the river from many years in th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ons. “Does this mean the factory broke a rule?” Ruby asked Officer Su. “Not yet,” the officer said. “We need to read the whole paper and speak with the people involved. Remember that a missing page is not proof of a bad act.” Mia wrote that under FACT, not GUESS, because it was a rule for how they would work. Ms. Kao waved from the door. “Try the city records room,” she called.

chapterReports.title: 水不是海來的
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The science teacher took the class to a safe place above the river. She held two small cups and asked a question: “Does river water always stay the same?” No one gave a sure answer. “Sometimes the sea moves into a river,” she said. “Sometimes water comes down from the hills. How can we tell?” She gave each team a simple test with salt. Mia rode her bicycle to school that day and had left it by the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: rote what they still needed: the full gate rule, the old test book, and an answer from the factory. Her father came into the room with two cups of tea. “You know,” he said, “when I was young, I also thought every problem had one right answer.” Mia looked up. “And now?” “Now I think finding the answer is only the second part. The first is learning to ask without hurting people.”

chapterReports.title: 檔案室的第二張圖
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mia went to the city records room with her father and Officer Su. She had never been there before, though the city was only a short train ride away. “What is the age of this building?” she asked while they waited outside. “More than a hundred years,” her father said. “People have used it for records for a long time.” Mia felt small beside the high stone gate. It was difficult to imagine so many ye

chapterReports.title: 市場的水管

chapterReports.title: 她劃掉的那一條

chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The café beside the station had bright windows and six different kinds of tea. Helen chose a seat facing the door. I told him that cake crumbs would not destroy his future.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: plete papers required a new review. It was not the full correction I wanted, but it was the first official sentence that did not begin by calling my father guilty. I read it to Adrian. He did not tell me to be happy. He asked whether I wanted to call Mother. I did. She answered on the second ring, already awake, as if she had been waiting five years for this particular morning.

chapterReports.title: 舊檔案上的印章
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mother read the findings at the counter while the street woke around us. The baker arrived with fresh bread. The bookseller brought the bill for the window boards and refused to let me call it a gift. "A fair price is easier to remember," he said. I paid him from the first nurse order. The small exchange pleased Mother more than any speech about a successful launch. Our store had work. It had debt
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: in by asking one frightened person to face the company alone. Adrian called Rose. Owen asked the woman to meet us with the workers she trusted. Mother made more tea. I moved the table toward the window, where the light was better. The first line I crossed out had been about owning my designs. The next line would be about who was allowed to own the truth of somebody else's life.

chapterReports.title: 安靜的點子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In Shell Bay, the summer fair was always loud. Sela, a young capybara who liked drawing, saw her small neighbor cover his ears near the music. She asked why everyone had to enjoy the fair in the same way. She wanted to make something gentle, but she did not know where to start. A small bug crawled along the empty wall of the hall. Sela wondered whether this corner could become a quiet place for ne
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: The woman smiled and asked when she could come back. Sela could not give her a date yet, so Uma offered to bring the news when the plan was ready. Then Daro put the fish flat in a box. They would use it again, but first they needed to ask about the hall. Sela looked at the white cloth one last time. This was no longer only an idea in her head. Someone was waiting to hear more.

chapterReports.title: 一座廳堂，許多聲音
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning, Uma led Sela and Daro to the town office. A goat named Oren cared for public rooms. He listened to their idea and showed them the hall rules. The hall could be used for a free event, but the friends had to leave it clean and safe. Uma said anyone could come to the town office to ask about public rooms. Oren lived in a small apartment above the office with his family. Sela wanted
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: erious part of the plan, not a small job to leave until the night of the show. Sela wrote three tasks on a clean page. The first was the story, the second was the room, and the third was asking neighbors what they needed. Oren had given Uma his office phone number. She placed it beside the room plan. They now knew whom to ask when a question was too large for the three of them.

chapterReports.title: 牆上的魚
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the third day, Daro brought a paper fish to the hall. He held it close to the lamp, and its shadow grew so large that only half of it showed. When he moved it back, the fish became very small. The friends learned that the space between light and paper mattered. All the friends watched the paper fish change size in the light. Uma marked an area on the floor where the table could stand. A basketb
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nobody would need to guess. Daro put the larger fish beside the first one. From near the table, the older fish still looked lovely. From the back chairs, its face disappeared. Sela kept both rather than throwing one away. They showed why the change was needed. 'I will watch from the back next time,' she said. The guests would see the fish; she needed to see what the guests saw.

chapterReports.title: 敞開的門
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Before they built more figures, Uma asked everyone to look at the hall entrance. There was a high step near the door, and one chair stood in the way. Some guests might need a wide, clear path. Sela had been thinking about the screen, not about how people would reach it. The side room had a bath, though visitors only needed its sink to wash their hands. One old chair could block the path if they le
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he guest reached a chair without asking anyone to carry her things. That was a happy surprise for Sela. She had spent so long looking at a fish that she had forgotten how much a doorway could matter. They would pass the plan to Oren before calling the room ready. For now, Sela added the guest's question to her notes: could she find the same clear path when every chair was full?

chapterReports.title: 紙、光與計畫
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Sela wanted to make a story about a fish who thought the sea was too wide. The fish would meet other small animals and learn to ask for help. Daro liked the idea, but he said that too many scenes would take time. They decided to make three simple scenes and test each one. The small bank near the market opened before the friends started their work. A farm outside town offered old clean card boxes f
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: to finish it before going home, but the fish's loose mouth could wait. Their last topic was where to put each figure so the next day's work would begin without a long search. Daro drew the box on the plan and added a small mark for the fish. Sela put her pencil down. She could see tomorrow's job, and she did not have to do it tonight. The three scenes would grow one at a time.

chapterReports.title: 一場表演的代價
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: When the friends counted their supplies, they found only enough card for a few more figures. Sela wanted to buy bright paper and more lamps. Uma asked how they would pay for them. The show was meant to be free, so they could not use money they did not have. Daro lifted his arm to show the friends a sheet of clean card. Uma said the nearby store was convenient because they could walk there together
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: oke in the next test. A gift did not have to be used if it could not do the job. The owner showed them another piece of cloth, but they did not take it before checking their money. On the walk back, Sela carried a smaller bag than she had hoped for. It was enough to start. At the door she turned the sign outward: every guest would be welcome, not only the people who could give.

chapterReports.title: 西邊的故事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Sela did not want to tell only her own story. She visited the homes near the west beach and asked what scenes people remembered from childhood. Some were ready to talk; others wanted to keep their memories private. Sela thanked both groups. A story was a gift, not something she could take. Sela made notes by the shore while listening to the neighbors' stories. A child brought one square of chocola
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: chose something different. There were still three scenes to start with, and a funny fish with a new hat. Daro set the hat gently on the table while Uma read the names on the idea cards. Sela could hear the sea through the window. She had walked west looking for stories to bring home. Now she understood that listening also meant leaving some stories where they already belonged.

chapterReports.title: 老物件之屋
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A small museum opened only twice a week near the town square. Sela, Daro, and Uma went there to learn how people had made pictures long ago. A guide showed them simple shapes cut from thin wood. The shapes looked very different from their paper fish, but the idea of light was familiar. Uma borrowed a book about old ways of making shadows on cloth. Daro thought the first room was boring until he sa
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: would have to try it. Uma said she would tell the guide what they learned and name the museum when they described the method. A train passed beyond the square, making the friends stop talking for a moment. When it was quiet again, Sela asked about their next fish. Uma smiled. 'You can make that story your own,' she said. 'We borrowed a way to move, not a life to put on stage.'

chapterReports.title: 安靜並不容易
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The friends invited a small group to watch their first linked scenes. Sela thought a silent show would be easy for everyone. She was wrong. A visitor who could not see the thin lines well asked for someone to say what was happening. Another visitor wanted less talking. Their wishes seemed to pull in different directions. A bear visiting the hall asked where to sit for the spoken version. Sela felt
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: answer had grown from more than one voice. Sela drew a line between the two times to show that guests would not need to listen to the spoken part if they chose the quiet one. A warm room was not only a room with warm air. It was also a place where someone could say what did not work. Before she closed the hall, Sela asked the visitors whether she had understood them correctly.

chapterReports.title: 小小的燈光開關
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Daro built a small box to hold the lamp, but its switch was hard to find behind the screen. During practice he reached too far and knocked over a paper figure. Sela stopped the scene. They needed a safer way to change the light, especially while people were moving in the dark. Uma looked around the lamp table to find the hard-to-see switch. Daro tested a large button that was easy to feel with one
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: y Sela had called a stop. Uma usually checked the doorway before the room went dark, and she asked them to leave time for that check in the play. Daro made a mark beside the light change. They did not want to worry a guest who stood up at that moment. Sela tried the move once more. The little button had not made the story more exciting. It had made room for the story to happen.

chapterReports.title: 給每位客人的座位
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Uma invited several neighbors to try the seats during a short practice. A young bird wanted to sit near the screen, while an older goat asked for a chair with a back. Someone needed room for a walking stick. Sela saw how much care was needed before the first figure even moved. Uma brought a basket of clean cloth for people to use at the hall. Daro put his belt on a hook so it would not catch on a
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he fish's short journey. She kept moving the figure rather than turning toward every person who stood up. From the last row, the fish still showed clearly against the white cloth. One visitor came back smiling. She had taken the break she needed and had not become part of the show. Sela put the two extra chairs in the side room. More chairs did not always mean a better welcome.

chapterReports.title: 節目單上的名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town asked Sela for a simple program. She wrote the story title but did not know whose name should appear under it. She had drawn the first fish, yet many neighbors had helped. Daro made the figures, Uma planned the seats, and others shared ideas that they had allowed the group to use. A young actor offered to read a short line for the spoken show. The group met in the afternoon to decide how
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: name could still be added before the next printing; a private name could still be taken out. Near the bottom, Uma wrote that each ticket cost nothing. Rich and poor neighbors would enter by the same door. Sela put the program beside the first fish drawing. The fish had begun with her pencil. The longer page beside it showed how far it had traveled through other people's hands.

chapterReports.title: 窗邊的測試
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The afternoon sun came through a wide window and made the shadow fish hard to see. Daro thought the lamp was broken. Uma looked carefully and found that the bright window, not the lamp, was the problem. They decided to test the show at the same time of day as the festival. The fish shadow looked beautiful when the bright window was covered. Daro used a brown card to make the shell keeper stand out
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ssed the white space. Daro stood beside the window and asked her to call when the shadow became hard to see. Uma wrote down the time of that change. The room, the light, and the chairs had to work together; a good fish shape could not do everything by itself. At sunset, Sela took the window cloth down. They would put it up for the next test, with the same clear space around it.

chapterReports.title: 小傷與更好的規則
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: During a fast practice, Daro turned and hit his arm on the corner of a table. The hurt was small, but everyone stopped at once. Sela felt afraid that their work was becoming too rushed. She asked Daro if he wanted to sit down and said they would not go on until he felt ready. An ant walked across the table just before the fast practice began. Daro kept his bag under a chair, far from the walking p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: down the total time from the first light to the last shadow. It was shorter than before, because nobody had to stop and pick up a fallen thing. Sela asked Daro how his arm felt before they began again. She wanted his answer, not only a faster number on Uma's page. The next practice would use the new route. Tonight the figures stayed in their boxes while Daro went home to rest.

chapterReports.title: 兩種說故事的方法
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The friends still had to finish the fish’s spoken lines. Daro wanted funny voices and a busy show. Uma wanted words to be few and clear. Sela liked parts of both plans. They talked for a long time without finding a choice that pleased everyone. The festival day was getting close. The little fish looked up at the light above the screen. Sela wanted to show care for guests who liked different kinds
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: The story could still be followed in both ways. They had already tried the idea with a few visitors; now they had to make both versions clear enough for festival night. Sela drew a small fish beside each time on the program. It was the same fish twice, taking a journey that guests could enter in different ways. She left room between the times for everyone to move without hurry.

chapterReports.title: 海邊傳來的歌
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: An old sea turtle named Hedo visited during practice. He heard the friends speak about the quiet show and said he knew a gentle song from his youth. Sela asked him to sing a little. The notes rose and fell like the waves outside, and the room became still. The bright evening sky made the sea look silver near the hall. Sela wanted to change the music only after asking Hedo's permission. Hedo said h
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nt, and the spoken version would name where the song came from. Uma showed Hedo the new line in the program. He read it slowly and asked her to keep his mother's place in the story of the song. She did. Outside, the sea was very quiet beneath the evening sky. Hedo began the tune again as he walked home. This time Sela did not reach for her pencil. She simply listened to him go.

chapterReports.title: 完整試演
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The day of the first full test arrived. Uma asked everyone to come early and stand in the right place. Daro laid out the figures in the order they would appear. Sela checked the script and took a seat at the back. For the first time, the whole play would run from beginning to end. Sela said the best time to test every scene was before the festival day. Daro helped build a simple stand to keep the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ney. It had given the next scene time to be seen. They would test that change once more before printing the final program. Daro asked whether taking something out could really make the play better. Sela pointed to the two figures, now waiting within reach of his hands. The wise choice was not always to make more. Sometimes it was to let the part they already loved become clear.

chapterReports.title: 明天的備用箱
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Two days before the public test, a small part of the shell puppet broke. Daro had made it from old paper, and the edge was weak. He looked upset. Sela told him they could fix it, but she also asked what would happen if something broke during the real show. The room fell quiet. Daro found a long strip of tape along the edge of the work table. A bad tear in the old paper made the shell figure hard t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: er show one day. Sela smiled, but said they first had one festival to prepare for. Uma put the box on the list beside the other things to check before leaving. Sela asked them to wake her only for a real problem tonight. The spare materials could wait safely here. On the way home, she was able to think about dinner instead of trying to carry every broken paper tail in her head.

chapterReports.title: 最後一班回家的公車
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Uma learned that the last bus left the bay earlier than she had thought. Two helpers lived far from the hall and could not stay until night. Sela first wanted to ask them to work later anyway. Then she remembered that a show should not make the people who helped it lose their way home. Daro wanted to become a better helper, not someone who always worked late. One tired helper said he needed to get
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: jobs that remained. Daro used a soft tie around the spare paper and put it within reach for tomorrow. Without the noise of moving chairs, Sela could hear the bus leave. For a moment she wanted to call everyone back and try the lights again. Instead, she checked the list. That test was finished. The helpers had done what they promised, and now they should be allowed to go home.

chapterReports.title: 空空的椅子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the day of the open practice, Sela arrived early and checked every chair. The lamp worked, the figures were ready, and the door stood open. But no visitors came. After half an hour, Daro asked if everyone had forgotten the event. Sela felt her face grow warm with worry. At first, no guests appear at the open practice, and Sela feels worried. The chairs stayed empty because the sign outside show
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: atch. Afterward, the friends shared soup and read the guests' questions. Daro added a round fish eye to the corrected sign. Sela checked the date herself before he put it outside. Yesterday she had looked at empty chairs and heard failure. Today there were six different voices to answer. A wrong sign had not told her whether the story mattered. It had told her to read the sign.

chapterReports.title: 公開會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Five days before the festival, Oren held a public meeting about the hall. Some people wanted to use it for storage. Others had seen the open practice and hoped it could stay a place for neighbors. Sela listened carefully. She knew that loving an idea did not give her the right to decide for the whole town. A small group of neighbors came early for the public meeting. Uma said the hall should alway
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: plan had to make space for things as well as for people. Daro asked again whether this meant they had won. Sela looked at the teacher measuring a table and at Oren checking the storage door. Nobody had got every room for themselves. They had found a way to begin. She gave the teacher a blank idea card. There would be other stories here after the fish had gone back into its box.

chapterReports.title: 地板與燈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town sent an engineer to check the hall before festival day. She looked at the floor, the doors, the tables, and the lamp. Sela was nervous because she had never planned an event this large. The engineer explained what she was checking and asked the friends to show their plan. The engineer said the group had the ability to make small safe changes. No one left clothes on the floor near the exit
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: yone to come inside. Daro pointed to the second performance time on the program. A guest could wait for that one instead of standing in a doorway. The engineer's notes would stay with the room plan. When the hall was used by another group, they would not have to guess why a shelf had been moved. Sela put the plan by the door, ready for people rather than only for the inspector.

chapterReports.title: 年輕的小藝術家
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: During the last school visit, a small child named Nemi watched the fish meet the shell keeper. Nemi raised one hand and said the fish should not simply be given the way home. It should learn to ask another fish for help. Sela had not thought of that ending, and she liked it. Nemi wanted to act out a short part of the fish story with a paper figure. The child's action made Sela see the ending in a
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: fish move faster for festival night. Sela said this practice was a chance to study what people understood, not only what they could make the figures do. They tried the same short part again. Nemi could follow it without the teacher explaining. When the group left, Sela kept the child's name beside the new scene. An idea could be small and still change where a whole story went.

chapterReports.title: 節慶之夜
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Festival evening finally came. Neighbors arrived with bags, light jackets, and happy faces. A few visitors needed help at the entrance, and Uma showed them the clear path. Sela stood behind the cloth and heard the gentle sounds of people taking their seats. She was afraid of making a mistake, but she was ready to begin. The hall was almost full when the first guests arrived for the festival. A fam
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the open path to the door. The price of a seat had stayed zero, just as they had promised. 'We can put the cloth away tomorrow,' Daro said. Sela agreed. Tonight they only needed to leave the room ready for the people who would open it in the morning. Outside, louder music still came from the fair. She could enjoy hearing it now, knowing that the hall had offered another choice.

chapterReports.title: 留給新故事的地方
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: During the last week of the trial month, the town held a meeting about the hall’s future. Oren brought the notes from the one-month trial plan, and neighbors shared what they hoped to do next. Sela came with Daro and Uma. She was not afraid to speak, but she was careful not to speak for everyone else. The friends were able to teach new groups how to use the screen safely. Sela was no longer afraid
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ow of her own. Other neighbors would have their turn to lead. On the empty program cover, she wrote one word: Together. Below it she put the names of the friends and helpers who wanted to be named. Then she closed the book. Tomorrow a different person could open the door and find enough room for a different story. Sela walked home with nothing left to prove on the little stage.

chapterReports.title: 第一聲鈴響
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At six thirty a.m., the bell above the post office door made a soft sound. Ada was early for her first day as the town's new mail worker. The morning sun was warm, but the bag of letters was heavy. Mr. Lee, the old postman, was ready to teach her the roads. He put a cover over a box near the window. “That box is for letters that need a new address,” he said. Ada wrote this in a small blue book. On
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e letters for today were all in the right hands. Mara still had her red envelope and the choice to keep it closed. Ada felt tired and happy at the same time. She did not know whether the old house was still standing. She did know that tomorrow she could learn one more road, carry one more letter, and listen to one more person. Outside, the bell moved gently in the evening wind.

chapterReports.title: 河邊的清單
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada's cousin Tom came to the post office with a map of the south side of town. His family had lived beside the river for a long time. “I can bring you some new street names,” he said. “I can also help carry the empty boxes, but I will not read anyone's mail.” Ada smiled. Tom was a helpful guy, even when he talked too much. The sun was bright and the day was sunny. They put the map on the desk and
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: first and check the new house numbers one by one. Mara could come to the library, where Tom would show her the old video. Nobody needed to hurry. The river had changed its path over many years; people needed time to find their way too. Ada put her work shoes by the door and left the public map on her desk. She was learning that a list could make a hard day easier for everyone.

chapterReports.title: 海灘邊的路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Wednesday, Ada learned about the road from the station to the beach. Mr. Lee said the road was far from town, but the walk was safe in good weather. A little bird sat on a sign near the bridge. A cow stood on the other side of a fence. Ada cleaned the dust from her shoes before entering the first house. The owner had been born in this town and had lived there for nearly every year of her life.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: names, and people who needed more than a quick delivery. She made three clear notes for tomorrow. First, check the public dates on the maps. Second, leave private letters closed. Third, give a person time to ask a question. She could not solve every problem on the same day. Still, the road had brought her closer to the people who lived beside it, and she felt ready to go again.

chapterReports.title: 小鎮廣場
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A boy ran across the town square with a butterfly on his school bag. He nearly dropped a letter when a strong wind began to blow. Ada caught the paper and helped him put it away. A tall worker from the old factory watched them. “Thank you, sir,” the boy said. The worker shook his head and smiled. He had come to ask about mail service for the factory staff. Some workers could only visit after their
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: box. The market wanted a clear place for lost cards. Some older people wanted help reading street numbers. None of the ideas was large by itself, but together they showed what the office meant to the town. Ada took off her wet shoes and placed them by the door. She would not promise everyone an answer tomorrow. She would promise to ask, write, and return with what she learned.

chapterReports.title: 花園裡的記號
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Although it was warm in town, the hills were still cold. A small patch of snow lay beside the garden near Willow Road. Ada and Mara went there to look at a public stone marker. They did not dig, because the land belonged to another family. A frog jumped into a pool, and a hen walked past a row of beans. “This is a long way from the river,” Mara said. “Maybe the road moved, but the garden stayed.”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t delivery, stop at the school office, and ask whether the old public map could be seen. She would check the date and write down the part that mattered. Then she would tell Mara exactly what she had found, not what she hoped to find. It was a long plan for a small stone, yet Ada felt at peace. She was beginning to understand that care could be quiet and slow, and still be real.

chapterReports.title: 舊屋旁的小船
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Before Ada could leave the post office, a small boat arrived at the river landing. It carried a box of letters for the houses across the water. The road to those houses was closed for work, so the boat driver had agreed to help. Ada checked the box before she took it. “I cannot drive a boat,” she said, “but I can see that the names are right.” The driver waved to her and showed her a sign on the l
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: eliveries, but it could not replace every road. Someone had to check the weather, the times, and the cost. She also wrote about the man at the landing, using only what he had said in public. She kept Mara's choice out of the work book. Ada was still new at this job, yet she knew that a good worker needed more than strong arms. She needed to listen, ask, and know when to say no.

chapterReports.title: 時鐘與雨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: As the clock reached eight, rain began to tap on Ada's bedroom window. She had a dream about letters flying over the town like birds. She woke with a laugh, then heard a strange noise outside. The old yard gate was moving in the wind. It was not a person trying to get in. Ada closed it and went back inside. She believed a good morning began with one clear look at the facts, not a guess made in fea
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: given one woman a fair choice, and carried every letter on her route. She had not found Mara's old house, and the office still faced a question about its future. Yet the day had not been empty. She wrote a short note beside the clock: “Do what is right today. Ask about tomorrow when tomorrow comes.” Outside, the rain washed the yard clean, and the town grew quiet for the night.

chapterReports.title: 公園的一天
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town held a baseball game in the park. Ada did not need to work all day, but she had a short delivery to make. A girl in a red dress waited outside the gate for a birthday card. Behind her stood a group of children with different colored hats. “Can you give this to my grandmother?” one child asked. Ada explained that he could place it in the post box, where it would follow the right route. “Th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the people more than the score. She had made a delivery, protected a man's privacy, and shared lunch with Mara. The old post office was a small place in a larger town, yet its work touched many lives. Ada wanted the city office to see that. She decided to ask Mr. Lee whether the town could keep a clear record of the ways people used the service, not only the number of letters.

chapterReports.title: 節慶明信片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The autumn festival was coming, and Ada's bag was full of cards. On the way back from the lake, she met a grandmother who had made a dish of rice and banana for her family. “Please take this card to my sister,” she said. Ada checked the street and number. “Okay,” she answered. The woman asked Ada to stay and eat, but the delivery was not finished. Ada promised to visit after work if she still had
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t she remembered one quiet scene best: Mara folding her note and choosing what to keep private. The town could give her maps and stories, but not the right to take that choice away. Ada put the next day's mail into order before going home. She felt ready for the city office's letter, which might arrive soon. Whatever it said, she wanted to answer with real work and clear facts.

chapterReports.title: 聽得見的文字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: An apple fell between two trees near the town center. Ada picked it up just as a boy ran past with a ball. He was playing with his brother, who was blind. The older brother knew the way by the sound of his feet and the line of a low wall. The boy wanted to kick the ball near the wall, but Ada asked him to move the game. “Your brother has the right to walk here safely,” she said. They agreed to pla
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ght worrying, or she could take simple steps with the people who used the office. She chose the second way. The brothers had shown her something important that morning: one service did not fit everyone in the same way. A town office had to listen to each person and make room for different needs. Ada did not feel ready to win a big fight, but she felt ready to begin a fair talk.

chapterReports.title: 藍色的門
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The weather turned cold, and Ada found a blue car beside the office with a flat tire. A nurse stood near it wearing warm pants and holding a bag. “I need to be at the temple before noon,” she said. “I cook for the older people there on Fridays.” Ada could not fix the car herself, but she could call the repair shop. Mr. Lee asked whether the woman needed a safe ride first. A driver from the next st
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: rong about a number and correct it, but she did not want to be careless with people's lives. The office was small, and the city might see only a few rows on a page. Ada wanted each row to tell the truth. Mara's red envelope waited in the drawer where she had chosen to keep it. Both women were looking for something from the past, but they could still do good work in the present.

chapterReports.title: 兩種語言的信
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada rode her bicycle to the school because a teacher had asked a question about mail. A family at the school spoke a different language at home. Their child wanted to answer a letter but did not know every English word. The teacher said the child could use his own language too. Ada bowed to the family when she met them and asked what help they wanted. “We want to write the address right,” the moth
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e words the children had written. Not every sentence was perfect, but each one was a real message from one person to another. She wanted the city office to understand that part of the work too. A town post office could be a place where a child learned to write to a friend, and where an older person learned a new way to ask for help. That work did not fit neatly into one number.

chapterReports.title: 柳樹路的門
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Many years ago, Willow Road had been part of the city road, but now it was a small lane. Ada and Mara found the old gate after walking from the hotel. Mara had borrowed a public map from the library, and Ada carried her own copy. Behind the gate stood a house with a blue door and a rock by the steps. “It looks the same,” Mara said softly. Ada understood why she felt that way. Still, they had a rul
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t about local service. The number of people at the office was small on some days, but the work outside town was large. Ada stood by the desk, thinking about all the places she had walked. She wrote, “Ask everyone who wants to speak, but do not count a person twice for the same visit.” She wanted the report to be fair. A true number was better than a large number that was wrong.

chapterReports.title: 蘿絲阿姨的花園
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada and Mara were already at the town hall when Aunt Rose came in. She was an older woman who ran a small garden business. She had agreed to show them a public book of street names. “I can tell you what I remember,” she said, “but memory is not always the same as a written record.” Ada liked that clear warning. Rose opened the book to the first page about Willow Road. She wore gloves because the p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ” she said. “You water it, and you come back.” Mara laughed at the small lesson. Ada looked at the fruit in her hand and thought about the post office. Perhaps a local service was like a tree too. It needed care, time, and real work to stay strong. She put the lemon in her bag, making sure it did not touch the letters. The day had given them a few more facts and one new friend.

chapterReports.title: 市場寄信日
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The morning market was busy again. Ada wore a simple T-shirt under her work coat and a hat against the sun. Her sister came to help set up a small table near the restaurant. They would show people how to send letters, but they would not take private mail without the proper box. “How many people will come?” her sister asked. “I do not know,” Ada said. “We have a job to do, not a number to chase.” A
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: smiling. “That is not a number for the city, is it?” she asked. Ada answered that smiles were not a formal measure, but they mattered to her. They could be one reason to keep doing the work carefully. At the corner, Mara stopped by a new tree. “Maybe the town is becoming part of my life now,” she said. Ada did not answer for her. She simply stood beside her friend for a moment.

chapterReports.title: 誠實的數字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada was angry when she saw a number on the report that was too high. Someone had counted each question at the market as a new visitor. The total was not correct. “I know it would make the office look busy,” she told Mr. Lee, “but it is not true.” He agreed. They sat with tea and a cookie and went through the notes again. The work took time, and the office grew warm from the heat of the small stove
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ote the date beside it and put the notes in order. There was no easy way to make the town office look large. It was a small office, and that was the truth. Yet a small place could do important work. Ada wanted the people who made decisions to see both facts. She closed the work book and opened the window. Cool air came in, and she felt ready for another day of ordinary letters.

chapterReports.title: 有兩個彎的道路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The morning air was cool, but a truck had stopped in the middle of the road. Its driver said the way ahead was closed for work. Ada had enough time to take another route, so she decided not to push through. A woman with a basket of vegetables asked if she could follow her. Ada showed her the public road map and gave an example of the new turns. “You go past the small tree and then turn right,” she
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e time spent using the safe route. She did not blame the driver for the delay. The road had been closed for a reason, and he had warned her. In her notes, she wrote about the fact, the action, and the result. She hoped the city office would see that good mail service was more than speed. Sometimes a short stop and a clear talk protected people and letters from a larger problem.

chapterReports.title: 學校寫信小隊
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ada was certain that the school could help the town learn about letters, but she did not want children to do adult office work. The school leader, Mr. Park, agreed. He asked each child to write to someone they knew. Their father, mother, or friend could be the reader. The children were not asked to show private words to the class. One group wanted to dance after they finished. Another wanted to ju
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: sent a note thanking the office for the school visit. The note was short, but Ada felt glad to read it. Her job was not to make herself a hero. It was to make the road from one person to another easier and safer. She turned out the light, thinking of the children who would one day write many letters of their own. The post office would be useful if it kept making room for them.

chapterReports.title: 箱子裡的蜜蜂
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A bee flew out of an empty box at the post office, and a dog began to bark. Ada stepped back. The dog was black, with one white foot, and its owner called it away. A child nearby wanted to catch the bee, but Ada told him to leave it alone. “It may bite or sting,” she said. “We do not need to attack it.” They opened the door and waited until the bee flew out. No one was hurt. Ada made sure the grou
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ity report could be asked at the next public meeting. She did not write that the office was safe forever, because nobody knew. She did not say it was already lost, either. She hoped people would come with real questions and learn what had been done. The bee had been a small surprise that morning; the harder problem was still in front of them. Ada was ready to meet it with care.

chapterReports.title: 漲高的河水
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rain fell hard through the night. By morning the river was a hundred shades of gray, and the water stood just below the safe level on the old bridge. Ada did not try to cross. She called the office and asked for the new road rule. A doctor at the small hospital needed a letter sent to the city. The doctor said it was important, but she also said nobody should risk a life to carry it. “Can we send
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ak when the storm passed. Ada finished the public road notice and gave it to Mr. Lee to check. Both women had moved forward without leaving safety behind. Mara had a new chance to hear about her mother, and Ada had helped the town through a hard day. The storm was not over, but the lights were on in the office, and people knew where to ask for news. That was enough for tonight.

chapterReports.title: 遠方寄來的信
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: An airplane passed over the town as Ada opened the post office. The morning was busy, but the sky was clear and light. A small box had come from another country. Inside was a piano book for the married couple from Willow Road. Ada checked the number on the box and put it in the right place. The couple came later with a little girl who was bored by all the waiting. Ada showed her a picture of the t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nd Mara said she felt close to her mother in a new way. The old house was no longer the only thing she wanted. She wanted to know the people her mother had known and the places she had loved. Ada listened while a soft light came through the window. She thought that the town might become a home for Mara, not because of one building, but because she was making her own ties there.

chapterReports.title: 小小機器人
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A baby was crying near the library door when Ada arrived. Its mother sat on a bench and held a bag of dry clothes. A child was playing with a bat and ball nearby, but the mother asked him to move away from the baby. The child did so. Ada had come to see a school program about a small robot that could sort toy letters by color. The teacher explained that it was not a real mail worker. The robot cou
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e thought about the baby from the morning, the child who had moved his game, and the small robot that stopped at the chair. Every one of them had needed a different kind of care. A good town gave people room to move safely and to learn. She hoped the post office could keep doing its part. She could not know the city's answer yet, but she could be proud of the work already done.

chapterReports.title: 改變的房子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: “Hello,” said Rose when Mara came to the garden office. “Come in if you like. The tea is fine today.” Mara thanked her and showed a copy of the old play photograph. Rose looked at the people and knew the name of one woman. “She was my wife's old friend,” said a man beside her. He pointed to a small pot in the photograph. It had belonged to the school, not the family in the blue-door house. Mara ha
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: dishes away. The office report lay on the table, ready to send in the morning. She saw the red envelope beside Mara's coat. It was still closed. Ada did not touch it. That simple choice felt as important as any number she had checked. A letter could be a bridge between people, but only when they chose to use it. She turned off the light and let the quiet home settle around her.

chapterReports.title: 最後的報告
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the date set by the city, Ada came to the office early. Rainy weather had made the road wet, but the safe path across the square was open. She took a copy of the report from the desk and checked each page. It had the number of visits, the hours spent on deliveries, and the public questions from the market day. She did not add anything that could not be checked. Mr. Lee gave her a small present:
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: family, with a story about her mother's school days. There was no new secret, only a memory of a girl who liked drawing on letters. Mara smiled and placed the picture beside the red envelope. “I am glad I came,” she said. Ada was glad too. They had both learned that the past could be honored without stopping life in the present. They turned off the light and waited for morning.

chapterReports.title: 門仍然開著
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The airport bus came into town on a bright morning. Ada had gone to meet the city officer at the station, not to catch a plane. Her boss stood beside her with the finished report. When the officer arrived, he did not try to make the moment look like a show. He opened the folder and read the decision in plain words. The small post office would keep its afternoon hours for another year. The city wou
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: write a new letter of her own instead. Ada understood. The old letter had brought Mara to the town, but the new one would carry her own words into the future. The door was still open when the last child said goodbye. Ada smiled at the people walking home, then turned the sign to tomorrow's hours. There would be more roads, more letters, and more ordinary days worth caring for.

chapterReports.title: 河上的紅繩
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A small village stood beside a river, north of the hills. Nia, a young otter woman, wanted to cross the old wooden bridge with her pet bird, Dot. In the middle of the bridge, she noticed a red mark on one board. A little bug slipped through the crack. Nia knelt to look more closely; the gap was wider than she had thought. Worried that the board was splitting, she took a camera from her bag and pho
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: came with a small bag and stopped before the sign. “Can I go to the river?” he asked. “You can look from the high path,” Nia answered, “but you cannot go onto the bridge.” He read the sign slowly and walked back. Nia felt hopeful. The rope had done its job, and the village could begin talking about a safer future. The hard part was still ahead, but nobody had to face it alone.

chapterReports.title: 繞遠路回家
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The old bridge was closed, so everyone had to take the hill road. A small apartment above the church was home to an old mouse. She could not walk far. Luma went to ask if anybody could bring her lunch. “I can do it,” said Bo. “But we must be clear about the route.” They drew a line around the deep pond and marked the third turn with a white stone. They did not want anyone to forget the way. In thi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: afe corner and saw that the cart could turn there without trouble. She made a note to keep that part of the path clear. She also asked Luma to check whether the old mouse needed food tomorrow. Luma was happy to help, but they agreed to ask others to share the next trip. Caring for a village meant making a plan that helpers could keep, not one that left them too tired to return.

chapterReports.title: 每個人的地圖
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: All the helpers met in an open area near the river. They wanted to begin with a map, not a hammer. Luma drew the houses, the field for basketball, and the garden with one orange flower. Bo put a lamp on the table so everyone could see the paper. Fern asked the team to define a safe path: a path that did not touch the old bridge or the soft river bank. Nia drew three paths, then used an eraser to r
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: throw the old map away, because it showed why some paths were no longer used. Luma added a small picture of the rest chair beside the hill. Bo marked the places that would need a ground test. Soon the map told not only where people could walk, but also where the team had questions. Nia was pleased that everyone could see both the answers and the things they still did not know.

chapterReports.title: 兩岸的一個選擇
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In the east part of the village lived Mrs. Pine, a green turtle who knew the river well. She gave both Nia and Bo a bowl of warm water after a cold bath in the rain. “You must not cross the old bridge,” she said. “Look at the water before you look at the wood.” Bo wanted a short bridge near her house, but a large fallen tree could block that place during a flood. Nia made a choice: they would stud
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: had shown him a different way to think. At the turn in the road, he met a child carrying a little bowl of water. The child asked, “Will you finish the bridge tomorrow?” Bo knelt and answered, “Not tomorrow. First we must make sure the place is right.” The child looked disappointed, but then asked if the path would be safe. “That is exactly what we are trying to learn,” Bo said.

chapterReports.title: 村子的共同基金
