chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The village had a little money in the bank, but not enough for a new bridge. A farmer named May offered wood from a tree that had fallen on her farm. She did not want to sell wood that the animals might later need for food or homes. Bo went to feed the farm animals and thanked her. He carried a yellow letter to Fern. The letter said exactly which wood May could give. Nia read it twice. There were
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: write the names. A piece of wood from May's farm went in the gift space. Sol's iron ring would go in the loan space when it arrived. Nails that no family could give went in the buying space. The plan was simple enough for children to read. When the workers knew where each thing came from, they could also know whom to thank and what had to go home after the bridge was finished.

chapterReports.title: 河流記得的事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Bo took Nia to the old village shop, where a long desk stood by the door. Inside a drawer was an envelope full of papers about the bridge's history. Some pages showed the river after a very deep flood. One old picture showed fish near the top of the bank. “The water may rise higher than you think,” Bo said. Nia held the papers with one arm and used her other hand to keep them dry. She wanted to fi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: om the moving water. “I would like to begin today,” he said, “but the ground is too wet.” Nia agreed and put the paper back in its cover. They walked to the meeting hall and told Fern exactly what they had seen. There was no great new story to tell, only a clear report. Fern said a short true report was worth more than a long story built out of guesses. Nia wrote that down too.

chapterReports.title: 柳樹下的課
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The children met by a large willow tree for a class about river safety. Luma, a rabbit, brought a list of places where people should not walk. She drew one flower beside each safe path. Bo brought a long piece of wood and let the children see the marks on it. “This is not a toy,” he told them. “It is a real tool for our work.” One child asked how many hours it would take to build a bridge. “More t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: maker. Then she chose two pictures that could help people find the safe path. She explained why she could not put every picture on the warning sign. “A sign must be easy to read quickly,” she said. The children were not upset. They made a little wall in the classroom for the other pictures. Nia saw that saying no to one idea did not mean saying no to the child who had made it.

chapterReports.title: 模型不能只靠猜
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Bo opened a book from the village library. The drawing inside showed how a bridge could hold a heavy cart. He said that a plan might look boring, but it could save lives. On the table were a fork, a roll of bread, and a file of old drawings. Each helper got one small job. Nia would count the wood. Luma would listen to people's needs. Fern would tell the village what was known and what was still an
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: rst posts. The young mouse named the places where children might put their hands. Fern wrote all four on the board. She thanked the mouse again for noticing something the older helpers had missed. The little animal stood taller after that. Nia saw that asking a question could make someone feel like a true member of a team. She took the list home to read before the next meeting.

chapterReports.title: 農夫的鐵環
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A bear farmer named Sol came from the far hill with a wooden box. Inside was a strong iron ring that his father had used to lift stones. “Keep it safe,” he told Bo. “I would be sad to lose it.” Sol had been lonely since his wife moved to another village for work, but he was glad to have a useful job. Nia took a photograph of the ring and wrote whose it was on a small card. A gift and a loan were n
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: in the village had felt alone during the long rainy weeks. The closed bridge had made it harder to visit friends, but working together gave them a place to meet. Nia thanked Sol for the shelf. He said he wanted to keep helping even after his iron ring was returned. Bo laughed and offered him a chair at the next planning meeting. Sol said yes before anyone had to ask him again.

chapterReports.title: 不施工的夜晚
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The sky became dark early in the evening. A cold sound came from the river, and leaves began to fall around the work table. Nia checked that the children had gone home. One little student had lost a button from his coat. She found it near a rose bush and gave it back. “You usually stay late,” Luma said. “Please go home tonight.” Nia looked at the wet path. She knew that staying longer would not he
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: set time. Bo and Luma were there already. They compared the weather report with the marks seen from the high road. The rain had stopped, but the bank was still wet. Fern said the team would use the day to mend signs and prepare tools. It was not the work Bo had hoped for, yet he agreed it was the work they could do safely. Nia began to trust this steady way of making decisions.

chapterReports.title: 白色的線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning, Fern brought a basket of tools. A thin white belt from an old bag was inside. Bo used it to show where the new rail would stand. “Check every mark,” he said. “A small mistake at the start can hurt someone later.” A player from the village ball team offered to lift heavy wood, but Fern asked about his health first. He had a bad knee and had been to the hospital last month. They ga
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: roles and tried again. It felt like a simple game, and some helpers laughed. Yet Nia saw that the same answer came from different people. If one helper was home sick, another could still tell visitors what to do. Fern said this was how a village kept a useful plan alive: more than one person had to understand it. They put the new pictures by the doors before the next rain came.

chapterReports.title: 每個包裹都有位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At two o’clock in the afternoon, the town engineer arrived with a package of drawing tools. An actor from the village play helped carry it to the hall. His glasses fell when he bent down, and Nia picked them up. “I can carry the small box,” she said. “But I am tired. May we rest first?” The engineer agreed. No one had to act like a hero. They would work more carefully after a short rest. The last
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ork, while a test showed what happened under set conditions. He smiled and said she had understood. Then he asked what she would do if the test gave a bad result. “Stop and change the plan,” she replied. He nodded. Nia felt she had learned more than how to build a bridge. She had learned how to tell the difference between hope and proof, and why both mattered in their own ways.

chapterReports.title: 一步一步來
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A brown duck called Reed joined the team at the new site. He had lived by the river all his life and could read the water well. “The rain is coming,” he said, looking at the high clouds. Bo put a wide board beside a window in the old work shed. The board would become a safe stair from the path to the bridge. Luma brought a chair for Reed, who had a sore leg. She gave him honey with warm water. “Yo
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ly, while the lower place had small waves. Nia wrote his words as an observation. She did not say it proved the new bridge would be safe in every storm. Bo thanked Reed for staying to watch from the safe shelter. As they left, the two workers who had argued walked together up the road. They were talking about tomorrow's measurements, not about who had been right the day before.

chapterReports.title: 誠實的清點
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A little ant walked across a bag of nails as Nia counted them. A chicken from the farm followed her, holding a bottle of water. “The clerk said there were thirty nails,” Luma said. Nia counted again. There were only twenty-eight. She wrote the total on a card and asked the clerk about it. “I made a mistake,” he answered. “I am sorry.” He offered to bring the other two nails. Nia thanked him for be
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: a worker needed one more nail tomorrow, the book would show how many were left. She gave the young helper with the sore knee a dry cloth for his hands and thanked him for his work. He said he liked helping from a chair and hoped to walk back to the river when his knee was better. Nia reminded him that there was no need to hurry. The work would still be there when he was ready.

chapterReports.title: 第一根柱子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The morning was lovely and clear. The workers chose the best chance to put the first posts in the ground. Nia took care not to enter the marked danger area. Bo said, “A great bridge begins with a small right choice.” Luma carried a gift from Mrs. Pine: a clean cloth to keep tools dry. In her pocket was a note from the turtle's daughter, who wanted to help when school ended. Nia felt pleasure at th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: h path. Nia asked why they needed both pictures and numbers. Bo said a picture showed shape, while a number showed how far something moved. If a post changed its place during a storm, the team needed to know. Nia looked at the new posts and hoped they would stay still. She also knew that hope was not enough, so she put the pictures into the book and planned to check them again.

chapterReports.title: 灰色的天空
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The sky changed from bright blue to gray before breakfast. Fern's grandfather had once kept a notebook about river levels, and she brought one page to the work site. He had used pink paper for the highest water marks. Nia held the page inside a clear cover. “The weather matters,” she said. “We will stop if the water gets too high.” A pig from the south farm helped move tools away from the bank. Hi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: k at the high path. Fern still chose to wait for the ground to dry before anyone moved heavy wood. Bo did not argue. He could see soft mud around the first toolshed step. Luma moved the rest chairs away from that spot. Nia wrote down this small change too. The weather had not broken the new posts, but it had shown them which places became hard to walk on when the rain returned.

chapterReports.title: 測試之前
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: After the rain, the best news was that the first posts still stood straight. Bo was excited, but he did not want to build the rest at once. “We need to test them,” he said. He made a small circle on the ground around each post and told everyone to stay outside it. Nia and her friend Luma wrote down everything they saw. They had some knowledge from the engineer, but not enough to guess. It was wise
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: esult, but it could confuse a reader later. She drew one neat line through the mistake and wrote the right name beside it. She did not hide the old writing. Bo saw the correction and said nothing more was needed. They placed the book on the table where the engineer could read it in good light. For Nia, this quiet work was a sign that the team was ready to hear an honest answer.

chapterReports.title: 十二袋沙
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The engineer came along the high path with a ruler, a box of tape, and a dozen bags of sand. He said the bags could stand in for weight during a safe test on land. Bo wanted to move them next to the posts, but he saw something sharp in the grass. He stopped and picked up a broken piece of metal with the right tool. “That could be bad for someone's foot,” he said. Luma put it in a closed case. Nobo
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: er it. She reminded the helpers not to invite visitors onto the bridge. “Can we watch from the hill?” a child asked. “Yes, if you stay in the marked place with an adult,” Fern answered. The child was pleased to have a safe way to be part of the day. Nia saw that limits did not have to shut people out. A clear limit could help people take part without coming too close to danger.

chapterReports.title: 不對的繩結
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Cool air came in through the window of the work room. Bo sat beside Nia with a cup of water. On the computer was a picture of the rope knots they planned to use. “This one looks quick,” he said. “But quick is not always good.” They practiced a short knot on a small piece of rope. Nia tried it again and again. A young mouse from the school came home early and asked if he could watch. His father had
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: o did not ask him to hurry. Nia thought of the young mouse's better drawing, and she was glad they had made that small change. They tied the practice load, checked the knot twice, and stopped when the engineer told them to stop. The new test passed on land, but Nia wrote the result in careful words. The team still had more checks to do before anything could hang over the river.

chapterReports.title: 繩子沒通過的那一天
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A round pool of water appeared on the hill path after heavy rain. The work team went out to look at the new posts, not the old bridge. An elephant from the mountain village had come to help with a test on dry land. He was big, but the engineer said his size did not make him a safe test weight. They would use the marked bags of sand. Bo thought the test would be exciting. “We might fail,” Nia remin
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: en taking the hill road and Mrs. Pine resting by the chair. Waiting was not easy for them either. Still, she could not ask someone else to stand on a bridge that had failed a test. She wrote a short message for the village: “We found a problem. No one was hurt. We have stopped work on this part. We will test a new plan.” She read it aloud twice to make sure every word was true.

chapterReports.title: 每位鄰居的橋
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The village club held a meeting about the bridge's new cost. A young mouse carried the book around the table, and a kind bear helped the older neighbors read it. The group did not want to miss anything. Nia showed how much money and work each part needed. Fern said that the new plan was good, but it would take another month to finish if the weather stayed wet. Nobody liked the delay, yet they knew
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: His mother was pleased. She had often taken the long road with a heavy basket, and a place to sit would help her. The mouse asked if he could make a little wooden sign for the bench after the bridge was finished. His mother agreed, as long as he used safe tools with an adult. The village had a new plan not only for crossing the river, but also for helping people wait and rest.

chapterReports.title: 工程師最後的檢查
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The engineer came back to the village with a new drawing. He had the ability to measure the bridge, but he still asked Bo to check the marks with him. “Mathematics is useful,” he said, “but a number cannot tell you everything about wet wood.” In the storage room they found a dead branch on the floor. It had fallen from an old tree after rain. The engineer told the team not to use it. Nia put it in
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: er the path was easy enough for an older animal with short legs. Nia told him what Mrs. Pine had said and showed him the changes they had made. He asked them to check one sharp corner again before opening. Bo wrote it down at once. Nia was glad he had looked at the path outside the bridge too. The new crossing would only be truly useful if people could reach it without trouble.

chapterReports.title: 水面上的線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The new bridge was big enough for the village path, but the last check was still important. Nia wore a cap over her hair and made a dark mark on a thick board. The mark showed where the water had reached after the last rain. Bo raised his hand and asked everyone to stop talking for one minute. Even his large ears were turned toward the wood. They heard no new sound. That was good news, but the wor
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: child watched from the safe hill and held up a drawing of a red star. Nia waved back. That star reminded her of the first warning on the old bridge. She hoped the new crossing would never need a red rope again, but she knew it might one day. A good plan included knowing when to close, not only when to open. They returned to the hall to wait for the last word from the engineer.

chapterReports.title: 第一次安全通行
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: They were almost ready. Nia took a careful walk along the new path and checked every sign. A little insect sat on a carrot leaf by the hill. A child wanted to take it home in a jar, but Luma asked him to leave it there. “It has its own place,” she said. On a small island in the river, a bird opened its wings. The bridge was not for that bird; it had never needed one. Nia looked at the quiet water
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ace. Some adults cried a little. Fern asked them to keep the path clear for others who still needed to cross. Nia helped put the work book in a dry box at the entrance. It held the first photograph, the old flood marks, the test results, and the final rules. She knew that the box would be used again every week. The bridge was open, and now the village had to keep caring for it.

chapterReports.title: 屬於大家的橋
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A week after the new bridge opened, Nia was able to walk to the far field with her friends. A small cat carried a doll and wore a blue skirt. Another child was afraid of the high water, so Luma did not push her. She allowed the child to wait and look from a comfortable seat. “Sometimes we need time,” she said. The child smiled and asked to see the map. Nia showed her the safe path and said that a
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he old broken board after many years. Nia said they might not remember the board, but she hoped they would remember the choice to stop when something seemed wrong. The mouse looked at the water and nodded. They returned to the village as friends and neighbors began another ordinary day. That was what the bridge was for: not one great day of opening, but many safe days after it.

books.title: 獸人村的第一間早餐店

chapterReports.title: 紅色的門
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the north side of Little Leaf Village, a small red house stood beside a path. Fia, a young fox woman, stopped there with her pet bird, Blue. She had carried a camera to take a picture of the empty house. In the middle of the door was a small wooden star. Her grandmother had made it many years ago. Fia wanted to use the house for the village's first breakfast shop. She could almost smell warm br
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: she said. "You may open the door tomorrow, but you must write down what needs fixing." Fia showed her the picture on the camera. Edda looked at the roof, the window, and the little star. "Good," she said. "A picture helps us remember what is here now." Fia put the key safely in her bag. They had not made any food yet, but the first breakfast shop had taken its first small step.

chapterReports.title: 鑰匙與池塘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning, Fia opened the old house. Dust lay on the floor, and a long sofa stood by the back wall. "Can anybody help me move this?" she called. Moss came in first. Pip arrived from his apartment above the little village church. He was late because he had stopped to help a child find a lost shoe. Fia did not mind. She asked them to look carefully before they moved anything. Behind the sofa
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: good food, but it also needed small, careful habits. She looked toward the pond once more. A light shone in Toma's little work house. He would be awake early tomorrow. Fia hoped that, before long, he could begin his hard days with a warm meal and a little time to rest. She did not forget the pen they had found behind the sofa. It now had a place beside the growing list of jobs.

chapterReports.title: 每株植物的位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Fia set a small lamp on the table and looked at her plans. She had marked all the work areas in the house. The kitchen needed space for bread, the front room needed tables, and the back garden needed water. Pip came with an orange plant pot and a drawing of the garden. "Let us begin with the plants," he said. "We have a few seeds, but we can grow more." Fia smiled. "First we should define what we
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: aces, found a table, and fixed a chair. There were still many empty lines. She was tired, but she did not feel afraid of them. Each line was only a question that could have an answer. She put the list beside the door for the next morning. When she turned off the lamp, the old wooden star was still easy to see in the moonlight. A shop was beginning, one careful choice at a time.

chapterReports.title: 兩只碗
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rain came from the east before breakfast time. It fell on the roof and made a small pool beside the door. Moss put a bowl under a wet place inside. "We must fix this," he said. Fia saw that the water came from a little block of wood near the window. They could not simply move the bowl and forget the problem. Both friends put on dry coats and went to the back of the house. A green leaf was stuck in
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: elp. He also said he would bring more flowers from his garden, but only after he had finished the work he had already taken. Fia smiled at him. A shop was built with hands, not wishes alone. As the sky became dark, the three friends crossed the road and went home together. At the cross in the road, Moss lifted his head and checked for a coming cart before the friends went over.

chapterReports.title: 黃色細繩
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the fifth day, Fia went to the bank with a small bag of coins. She wanted to know how much money the breakfast shop could use. The clerk helped her count each coin. It was not a large sum. Fia wrote the number in her book and drew a straight line below it. She would not spend more than she had. Outside, a teenager with a yellow scarf was holding a long string. He was trying to tie two baskets t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: bout fruit and with Toma about early opening hours. Each friend was bringing one part of the shop to life. Before turning away, she looked at the yellow string on her book. It reminded her of the apples on the road and the kindness that had followed. A simple offer could open a new door. She hoped her breakfast shop would be full of such offers, freely given and carefully kept.

chapterReports.title: 泥裡的字條
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A hard rain fell in the morning, and the path to the farm filled with mud. Fia stood at her desk and read the news from a small village paper. The farm cart could not come through the old road. Moss came into the shop with one arm wet and a worried face. "What do we do about the eggs?" he asked. Fia put the paper down. "First we find out whether Kit is safe," she said. "Then we can speak with his
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: to arrive. By evening she understood a larger need: the shop had to work even when the world did not follow her plan. She put a dry copy of Toma's note in her book. Next to it she wrote two words, "safe first." It was easy to say them when the sun was out. She hoped she would remember them when the next storm came. She turned off her light, ready to try again the next morning.

chapterReports.title: 花朵小課堂
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Pip came by the west path with a large basket of flowers. He was a rabbit who loved growing things. "There is one more job we can do," he told Fia. "We can teach a class about simple food plants." Fia liked the idea, but she asked when they would have time. Moss had to finish his bread, and she had to clean the kitchen. Pip made a list and put one hour beside the class. "We can start small," he sa
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: tiny pot in her hand. There was a single seed inside. It was not ready to become food, just as the shop was not yet ready for its guests. But a seed could grow with time, light, and care. The small class had shown Fia what the shop might become: a place where people did more than buy and eat. They could teach one another, share what they knew, and take something good back home.

chapterReports.title: 錯誤筆記本
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Moss kept a small book by his oven. Every time bread went wrong, he wrote down what had happened. It was not a boring book to him. It helped him remember heat, time, and the kind of flour he had used. One morning, a loaf came out hard as a stone. "Another mistake," he said. Fia did not laugh. She listened while he told her about the fire. "The oven was too hot," he said. "I will try less heat next
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: d slowly become a book of learning. It held bad bread and good bread, old notes and new answers. That was how the shop was growing. Its walls were still plain, and some chairs still needed work, but the people inside were becoming ready to share a table. Fia locked the door and looked at the wooden star above it. She hoped the next lesson would bring them closer to opening day.

chapterReports.title: 牆邊的熊
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A traveler came to Little Leaf Village on a cold morning. He was a bear from a far town, and he looked lonely beside the wall of the red house. Fia brought him a cup of warm milk. "We are not open yet," she said, "but you may sit here and rest." The bear looked sad. "I have walked a long way and lost my map," he said. "I do not know whose house I should visit." Fia asked his name. He said it was R
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: th path. His voice was not very strong, but it sounded happy. Fia stood with Moss and Pip and listened. The day had begun with a stranger beside a wall. It ended with a friend finding his way. Fia looked into the quiet house. Perhaps a good breakfast shop was not only a place where food was sold. Perhaps it could also be a place where people found courage to take the next step.

chapterReports.title: 第一張菜單
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first menu was ready by evening. Fia put it on the red door and stood back to read it. There were three foods: warm bread, sweet fruit, and potato soup. Moss had tested each one, and Pip had helped with the fruit. "This is interesting," said Edda, looking at the board. "But how will people know what you have left at the end of the morning?" Fia had not thought of that. She added a small space
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: op had become part of her days. She was tired, but the work no longer felt like a dream far away. There was a menu on the door, bread in the kitchen, plants by the step, and friends ready to help. She touched the wooden star, then went home. Tomorrow they would invite a few neighbors for their first small breakfast. It was not the grand opening yet, but it would be a real test.

chapterReports.title: 白色籃子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the day of their small test breakfast, Fia set a white basket beside the door. It held notes for visitors. "Please tell us what was useful and what was not," she wrote. Moss checked the oven twice, and Pip put fruit into thin slices. Mrs. Fern arrived with her child. She wore a blue belt and carried a picture of a kite. "My child wants to make one after breakfast," she said. Fia welcomed them,
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ike the door. "Thank you for asking about the food," she said. "My child felt safe here." Fia held the picture for a moment. The best part of the test had not been the number of bowls they served. It was learning that people could speak and be heard. She put the notes in a safe drawer. Tomorrow they would read them again and choose what to fix before the first real opening day.

chapterReports.title: 下午的票券
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In the afternoon, Lark brought a package to the shop. Inside were tickets for a village music day. A small band would play near the supermarket, and an actor would tell stories from long ago. "The music starts at three o'clock," Lark said. "Would you like to bring a little bread for the visitors?" Fia looked at Moss. The last test breakfast had been tiring. She did not want to ask him to do more t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ouse was not a stage, and the team was not a band, but they were learning how to work together. Every person had a part to play. If one was too tired, another could help, or the work could wait. She looked at the ticket once more and set it by the yellow string. The red house now held more than old furniture. It held memories and promises, and soon it would hold breakfast, too.

chapterReports.title: 寬橋上的雨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rain began as the first morning visitors arrived. It fell in long lines across the wide bridge. Fia could see the road through the kitchen window. Two ducks were trying to cross, and Toma went out to lead them back to the pond. "The water is high," he called. "Please keep children away from the bridge." Fia put a clear note on the door. Their first job was to keep people safe, even if fewer visito
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: han expected, but they had not lost the trust of their guests. People had seen a safe place to wait, an honest food board, and a team willing to help. "That is enough for today," Fia said. She wrote the story in her book and closed it. The house was quiet now, but her thoughts were full. A long morning of rain had become a lesson in how a small shop could serve a whole village.

chapterReports.title: 門邊的螞蟻
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On a sunny morning, Fia found an ant near a bag of flour. Then she saw several more on the floor. She did not want insects near food. "We must clean this room before we cook," she said. Moss put the flour into a closed box, and Pip checked every bottle on the shelf. Kit, who had come to help, wore shorts and carried a small brush. They worked carefully. Nobody tried to hurt the little ants. Instea
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: when needed." Moss read it out loud. "Only three lines?" he asked. Fia nodded. "They are easy to remember, and we can add more if we learn something new." Moss smiled and went home. The shop smelled clean, and the boards by the door were dry. Fia looked down. No ants were coming through the little space. She closed the door softly and went to see whether Pip was feeling better.

chapterReports.title: 真正的第一個早晨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the first real opening morning, the sun came above the hill like a warm gift. Fia put a sign on the red door: "Open for Breakfast." She felt a great pleasure when she saw Moss and Pip arrive on time. Pip had slept well and was ready to work again. Edda came with her daughter, who wanted to choose the first table. "You may sit where you like," Fia told them. "But please keep the path clear." The
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e floor was clean, the chairs were safe, and people had shared a warm morning inside. Moss and Pip joined her. "We did it," Moss said. "We started," Fia answered. The difference mattered to her. They had not reached the end of the work; they had reached the beginning of a new way of living together. She shut the red door for the night, glad to know it would open again tomorrow.

chapterReports.title: 從海邊來的書頁
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A bright morning came after the first week of work. Fia sat inside the red house and read the notes in her book. The shop had changed a great deal, but one matter still worried her: the road by the pond became unsafe in heavy rain. A gray pig named Grandfather Oak visited with a folded paper in his hand. He had worked on boats when he was young and knew the land between the village and the sea. "I
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: feel calmer. Grandfather Oak stood at the door with his map. "Keep a copy," he told her. "The sea and the hills teach us to look ahead." Fia thanked him and promised to return the original paper safely. She shut the door, then stood under the wooden star for a quiet moment. A good shop was not just a place for sunny mornings. It had to be part of the village on hard days, too.

chapterReports.title: 朋友的圓圈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Fia asked the village helpers to meet in a circle outside the shop. She wanted to build a small dry shelf in the back room, where food could stay away from rainwater. Toma said the idea was good, but he needed to test the wall first. Moss brought a pair of old boards, and Pip carried a bag of tools. Everyone was excited to help. A child came with a drum and played a short beat for the workers. "Th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nodded. The shelf was not a great new building, only one small answer to a real problem. It made her feel better about the coming rainy season. The friends left in pairs, talking softly as the evening light fell across the road. Fia put one final note in the book. She wanted the shelf to stay useful long after this happy work day, not just look good when everyone was watching.

chapterReports.title: 沒有來的公車
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: One morning, a bus did not come along the road at the usual time. Children from the school had planned a trip to the zoo, but the road near the hill was wet and hard to use. Their teacher brought them to the red house to wait for news. Fia had just made a dozen small bread rolls. "There is enough for a little snack," she said, "but first we need to know how long you may stay." The teacher explaine
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: needed to change. They needed more clean drinking cups, a place for wet bags, and a clear note about how many people the room could hold. Fia knew they could not help everyone in every case. Still, they could be ready to do something useful. She closed the book and smiled at her friends. Their shop was growing in ways they had never expected when they first opened the red door.

chapterReports.title: 烤爐旁的床
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A stronger storm came in the evening. The air was cool, and rain made a loud sound on the roof. Edda called Fia on the phone. Some people from low homes near the pond needed a dry place until village helpers could take them somewhere safe. Fia opened the red house with Moss and Pip. They carried chairs to one side and made space beside the oven. Fia brought a small bed from the back room for an ol
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ught her a cup of water and sat across from her. "We did not fix the storm," he said. "No," Fia answered. "But we gave some people a safe place while others did the larger work." She looked around the room. Wet marks were on the floor, and the tables were out of place. Tomorrow they would clean and begin again. For now, she was glad that their little shop had been able to help.

chapterReports.title: 風雨裡的熱湯
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In the morning, the storm was still strong. A wet elephant named Ben came down from the mountain road with a message from the village helpers. The river had made a wide pool beside the bridge, and nobody should try to cross it. Fia read the message out loud. "We will not go out," she told Moss and Pip. "We can make soup here for the helpers when they return." Moss put a round pot on the stove. Pip
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e door in the last light. Some things had gone wrong, but the shop had stayed safe and useful. Moss washed the pot, Pip counted the dry food, and Fia wrote down what they had learned. "Tomorrow we will ask about the bridge," she said. "Tonight we will rest." Nobody argued. The hot soup was gone, but the room still held the warmth of people who had worked together on a hard day.

chapterReports.title: 星星下的會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A week after the storm, the village held a meeting at the red house. Edda asked the helpers to sit around the long table. The shop was a good place for the meeting because everyone knew the way there. Fia brought bread and water, and Moss made a small pot of soup. A young mouse from the garden club came with a guitar. "May I play after we talk?" she asked. "Yes," Edda said, "but first we must work
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he road work would begin later in the week, and the music day would come next month. She felt good because each plan had a place and a person to care for it. She no longer thought she must do every kind thing herself. A village could grow when people shared the work, and a small breakfast shop could be one warm part of that life. She closed her book, ready for the next morning.

chapterReports.title: 玻璃上的價格
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Fia stood on the clean floor and looked at a new price board by the glass window. She wanted every customer to see the price before buying food. A young engineer from the road team had helped make the board stand straight. "You have the ability to change the numbers when food costs change," he said. "You do not need to make a new board each time." Fia thanked him. She was hungry after working all
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: d see it. Nothing great had happened, yet the room felt more open. Pip put the drawing of the dead flower in his garden book. "I will try a new place later," he said. Fia nodded. She understood that work was not about never losing anything. It was about learning, making careful choices, and giving people clear information. She shut the window before the evening air became cold.

chapterReports.title: 大小藝術日
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: After the rain season, the village held a big art day beside the school. Fia wanted the shop to take part, but she did not expect the workers to stop making breakfast for a whole day. They chose one simple action: children could draw a star, and the shop would put the pictures on a wall. Pip wore a green cap and held the paper. Moss brought a thick book to keep the drawings flat. The first child c
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t the meaning was clear. Fia left the paper where everyone could see it. She thought about all the different things that had happened since she first opened the empty house. Some days had been easy, others hard. Each had taught a lesson. Tomorrow they would prepare for the harvest meal, and the stars would stay on the wall to welcome every visitor who came through the red door.

chapterReports.title: 胡蘿蔔的一排
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The day before the harvest meal, Pip took Fia to a small hill behind the village. They walked carefully past a row of carrots. The ground was soft from the old rain, and Fia almost put one foot in a muddy hole. Pip held out a hand. "Take this way," he said, pointing to a dry path. Fia was glad to follow. A small insect sat on her jacket, and she moved it onto a leaf. The day was hot, but the wind
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: all the voices that had passed through the red house: neighbors, children, travelers, workers, and friends. Each had helped her understand what the shop could be. Tomorrow was a celebration, but it was also a thank-you meal. The food would be simple. The people around the table would be the special part. She went home with a light heart and rested for the long, happy day ahead.

chapterReports.title: 門上的星星
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The harvest morning was warm and bright. Fia was afraid she might forget something, so she opened her book and checked the list twice. Moss made bread, Pip prepared fruit, and Kit helped carry clean plates. A little cat arrived with a doll in a red skirt. She wanted to sit near the window where she could see the star above the door. Fia helped her find a comfortable place. "Are you able to see it
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: at the clean tables and at the garden beyond them. "We have a plan for another year," she answered. "We will need to keep learning." Moss smiled. "And we will have breakfast tomorrow." They laughed, shut the door, and walked home together. The star could not make bread, stop a storm, or choose for anyone. It only showed the way to a door. The people had learned how to open it.

chapterReports.title: 空白的牆
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At seven a.m., the school bell rang across the yard. Mia came early because the art club had a big job. The spring fair was still several weeks away. In the main hall, a silver wooden star usually hung over the door. It was the school's oldest prize, made by students many years ago. This morning the wall was empty. Mia stopped with her breakfast in her hand. She had fruit, a small cake, and water,
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: nds made three rules: ask before going into a room, move nothing without a teacher, and keep every clue in the book. After lunch they placed the yellow paper in a clear bag. They could not bring the star back that day. But they had a place to start, and they had a plan they all understood. The empty wall was no longer only a worry. It was a question they could work on together.

chapterReports.title: 河邊的影片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning was sunny. Mia's cousin Leo came to school with a short video on his phone. His family lived south of town, near a river and a field of sheep. Leo was a helpful guy. He was not famous, but he loved science and could make a broken light work with one small tool. “I made this video on Friday evening,” he said. “I was filming the river for my class.” He showed them the water, the gra
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: u draw that part?” Ben nodded. “I can also draw the road from school.” They added the river to the map and made the line between the two buildings red. It did not mean they had found the missing prize. It meant they knew one place the truck had gone. For the first time, the search was reaching outside the school gate. Mia felt both hope and fear, and she let both feelings stay.

chapterReports.title: 路上的腳印
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Wednesday, Ms. Lin took the club along the road to the sports house. They walked in a line and stayed on one side of the street. A station stood near the bridge. Across the road was a small farm with one brown cow and three white birds. Ben liked the birds, but Mia said they had work to do. “Every step matters,” she said. “Please follow our teacher.” The sports house was not far from a beach wh
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ” she said. Mia answered, “I wanted to go there, too. But if we forget our rule, people may stop helping us.” They passed the birds again. This time Ben did not stop. He drew a little bird in the corner of the map when they reached school. Under it, Mia wrote one sentence: “The truck went to the town hall after the sports house.” Now the road on their map had a clear next turn.

chapterReports.title: 廣場上的故事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town hall stood beside a large square. It was a tall building, made from an old factory. A worker at the front desk smiled when Ms. Lin came with the children. “Good morning, sir,” Mia said to the man. He told them that the hall now gave a free service to local schools: they could use its rooms for music and art. A small boy was waiting with his mother near the door. He held a paper butterfly.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he people who were helping them. The clerk, the worker, the woman with the plants, and even the boy with the butterfly had been kind. None had asked for money. “Our town is full of people who care,” Mia said. “We should care about them, too. We will ask the next person kindly, and we will listen to the answer.” The club walked back toward the school with one more name to check.

chapterReports.title: 七張標記
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Thursday, Ms. Lin showed the club a picture of seven signs used by the town hall. Each sign had a number, and the number told workers where to put things. “At least we know why our paper has a seven,” Mia said. “It may be a room sign, not a name.” Ben pointed at a photo of the stage. He could see a box beside a bean plant and a picture of a frog. Another picture showed a hen and three little ch
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: d up her hand. “Was the box heavy? What was its height? Where did he put it?” Ana added, “Did he see a silver star?” Ben smiled. “That last one is the most important.” They put the questions in order and asked Ms. Lin to look at them. A good question, Mia learned, was better than a loud guess. If they were careful and kind, even a slow search could lead them to the right place.

chapterReports.title: 拿鑰匙的人
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mr. Green did not arrive at school until nine. He had to drive his uncle to a small house near the water before work. When he finally came, he carried a box and a cup of coffee. The children waited with Ms. Lin by the office door. “You may ask me anything about the move,” he said. “But I am not sure I can remember every box.” Mia held up the picture of the star. Mr. Green looked at it for a long t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ame of a woman who helped with plays. “We can see her tomorrow,” the teacher said. “Please do not go to her house. We will ask her here at school.” Mia thanked him. She could see that every small answer was like a part of a long road. She did not yet know where the road would end. But she was learning to walk it with care, one step at a time, without leaving her friends behind.

chapterReports.title: 不準的時鐘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ana came to school with a new idea. As she lay in her bedroom the night before, she had been thinking about the video. “I believe there is an error in the time,” she said. “Leo's phone said six, but the school clock near the gate said five when he came home.” Mia could not believe it at first. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: matter more.” They made a new plan: one short meeting each day, and no calls to people after school without a teacher. chapterReports.title: 公園裡的比賽
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday, the school held a baseball game in the park. Mia's group helped serve lunch, so they brought bread, beef, and fruit. Jo wore a blue dress over her sports clothes because she had a play after the game. chapterReports.title: 奶奶的節慶卡片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Sunday, Mia went to visit her grandmother near the lake. The street was quiet, and the town festival was still more than a week away. Grandmother had been a teacher at the school long ago. She was making rice and a dish with bananas for lunch. “Come in and sit,” she said. “You look quite tired.” Mia told her about the silver star and the yellow paper. Grandmother smiled with joy at the old stor
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Bring it to our meeting tomorrow.” Mia felt a new kind of joy. chapterReports.title: 網路上的照片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Monday, the school teacher brought an old computer to the library center. She helped the club look at pictures online from past school shows. There were more than a hundred pictures, and the students could spend only half an hour on the task. Mia's brother Sam came to help. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: . “We should ask the play leader about it.” Ben put his pencil away. “I want to find the star,” he said, “but I also want to be right about how we find it.” Mia nodded. chapterReports.title: 藍色的教室紀錄

chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: if we never find it?” she asked Ben. “Then we will still know how to ask better questions,” he answered. Mia smiled. She did not want to stop yet. chapterReports.title: 行星教室
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Wednesday, the club got an answer. The storage room was open for one hour, and Ms. Lin could take them there. It showed a planet and a large bow made of blue cloth.

chapterReports.title: 校門上的規則

A man at the gate told her that the sign had been there for many years. “It was put up before you were born,” he said. “Children of every age used to bring things back without a note. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: up for a good idea without doing all the work alone,” she said. Mia sat by the window and read the notes from the past two weeks. chapterReports.title: 新漆
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday, the club met a woman named Mrs. Vale. She was Ana's aunt and worked with school plays. She had already told Ms. Lin that the star might need new paint. “I can help with the work,” she said, “but we must agree about what is safe.” The star was very old. The wood could break, and the silver color had begun to fall away. Mrs. Vale put on gloves and showed them a small piece of wood from an
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: r been a list of old prizes. The teacher said there was one in the school office. “We can read it next week,” she said. The children took a short rest before class. Mia looked at the silver color on her drawing and imagined the star above the door again. But she did not mark the mystery as finished. They still needed the object itself, not just a good idea of where it might be.

chapterReports.title: 市場裡的戲服
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Saturday, Mia met Ana and her sister at the town market. They had asked Ms. Lin for permission to look at a public show of old stage clothes. The hall was full of visitors from different places in the world. One woman wore a tall hat, and a man wore a bright T-shirt. A small animal mask hung above a table. The seller told them it was not expensive, but a costume with real silver paint would cos
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Mia wrote it down, thanked him, and told Ana she would ask Ms. Lin before anyone called. “You want to look everywhere,” Ana said, “but you know we should not go everywhere alone.” Mia smiled. “I want the star back,” she said. “I also want all of us to go home safely.” They walked through the market, carrying only their notebooks and the small food bags they had bought for home.

chapterReports.title: 安全的工作方式
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At school on Monday, a science teacher invited the art club to see a short lesson about heat. She did not know how old paint worked, and she was glad someone could explain it. A student had a sore kne
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: That made it special in its own way. chapterReports.title: 司機的筆記本
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Tuesday, the school driver came to talk to the club. His name was Mr. Hall, and he was married to a woman who taught music. He had a strong voice but a kind face. “I can give you one good example of how a mistake happens,” he said. “When I move many boxes, I sometimes put one in the wrong order.” He opened his notebook and showed the children a list from Friday. It had two long cases with the s
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: theater room?” The others agreed. Jo said she had learned something about strong feelings. “I can be upset and still listen,” she said. Mia smiled. Mia hoped they could give that trust back by being careful with the answer, whatever it might be.

chapterReports.title: 團隊會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Today was the day of the big school team meeting. The club leader, Mia, stood beside a table in the open hall. Mr. Green and Ms. Lin sat on one side, and the children sat on the other. A giant paper bird hung over the table, ready for the fair. Some younger children wanted to touch it and jump under its wings. Their father asked them to stop. “The art club needs space,” he said. Mia opened the boo
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the hall. She remembered the day the empty wall first scared her. Now many people were helping, and no one needed to be afraid of asking questions. “Our team has changed,” Ben said. “We used to run after every new idea. Now we stop and check it.” Mia smiled at him. “That is how we can finish this well,” she said. The star was not back, but they had learned how to work together.

chapterReports.title: 漫長的訪談
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Before the visit, Mia interviewed another student who had joined the theater club last year. He wore a black shirt and had a small dog waiting at home. chapterReports.title: 舊舞台下方
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The old theater room was at the front of a small building behind the school. A sign said that people from abroad had once helped make the stage. The building worker opened the door and led the club in. The room was dark, and the air smelled of old wood. “Stay with me,” he said. “Do not touch anything until I say it is safe.” There was a low space below the stage. Mia looked down but could not see
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: th an injury.” Her mother showed her a picture of a doctor helping people after a storm. “People can work together,” she said, “but everyone needs to know their part.” Mia finished her homework and wrote a short note of hope in the club book. chapterReports.title: 星星背後的卡片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next afternoon was busy. Two building workers came to the old theater, and the club waited by the door with Ms. Lin. Ben was a little bored, so he drew a plane, a ball, and a piano on a piece of paper. “I want to show you something funny,” he told Jo. She smiled but did not look. Her eyes were on the room. At last the workers got the smaller box out. They placed it under a bright light so ever
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: could help save things for the next school fair. “Yes,” Mia said. “You can join our new card program. chapterReports.title: 牆上的新位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next day, students from every grade came to see the star in its safe box. A baby brother sat with his mother on a bench near the hall, but only school workers could go into the repair room. Jo explained the rule to a younger child who wanted to climb up and touch the star. “It is old and a little weak,” she said. “We need to keep it dry.” Ms. Lin gave the club a new job: find a better place on
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: owed what they hoped to do, and then people with the right skills checked whether it was safe. The star stayed in its dry box that night. The children did not mind. It had taken many days to find it, and they did not want to lose it again by rushing. When Mia went home, she looked back at the empty wall. It was still empty for one more evening, but it no longer made her afraid.

chapterReports.title: 小卡片上的名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday, a woman came to the school office and said hello to the art club. Her name was Mrs. Reed. Her husband had helped make the silver star many years before. She brought an old picture and a note that belonged to him. “He never forgot that day,” she said. “He was so happy when the school said yes to his idea.” Mia was polite and asked if they could look at the note. The woman agreed. It told
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: iss on the top of the head, the way a grandmother might, and told her to keep asking good questions. Mia felt a little shy but happy. The story would end with people working together, just as the star had begun.

chapterReports.title: 下雨的園遊會
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Saturday morning was rainy, but the school fair was ready. The club had worked hard to finish its game, its art show, and its new sign. Mia used her cellphone to invite family members who lived across town. Ben had made a copy of the star story for every visitor. Jo and Ana put each item on its own table with a number beside it. A younger kid came in carrying a toy horse and asked whether he could
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: et she stayed until the last item was checked. “We have not lost anything today,” Ben said. “That is a fine way to finish.” Jo laughed. “Not yet! Tomorrow we have the last party.” Mia smiled and looked at the star once more. The room was different from the empty hall she had entered weeks earlier. It had the same walls, but now it held a new way of caring for things and people.

chapterReports.title: 屬於大家的星星
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Sunday, the school held a small party for everyone who had helped find the star. Mia's uncle came from the airport in the morning. He was a busy man, but he wanted to see the hall and hear the story. At the door, the children had made a paper king with a crown and a big smile. Jo said it was only for fun. “The star is not for a king or a boss,” Mia told the younger children. “It is for all of u
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e another mystery next year?” he asked. “Maybe,” she said, “but I hope we will not lose another star.” They laughed. Mia closed the club book. chapterReports.title: 七點的鈴聲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The bell above the shop door rang at seven a.m. Rina was early again. The sun was still low, and the street was quiet. She worked at a small food shop called Morning Corner. She liked to make breakfast for people who had no time to cook. She put fruit near the window and a fresh cake on the table. A man on the old couch held a bag against his chest. He was Mr. Park, the shop owner. He smiled, but
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ice calm. "You may look at my book," she told him. "I will write everything again tomorrow." Mark gave a short laugh and went away. Mr. Park stayed. Tomorrow she would begin with facts, not fear.

He could bring a broken lamp back to life with one simple tool. Today he brought his camera and showed Rina a short video. "I made this for our family," he said. "Look at the sheep near the river." chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: own hands," he said. "Ask the people who know that part of the work." Rina watched his boat move away. She knew she had needed Jo, May, Nora, and Tom. chapterReports.title: 慢了一分鐘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rina woke up in her bedroom before her clock rang. She had a dream about a room full of papers. In the dream, each paper had a mouth and made a loud noise. She laughed when she opened her eyes. Real paper did not speak. But a time on a paper could tell a story. She went to the shop and looked at the delivery times. One page said seven thirty. Another said seven thirty-one. There was only one minut
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: rowing pale. She knew not every beautiful thing could stay. A good rule, however, could last after the people who made it went away. chapterReports.title: 公園裡的遊戲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Sunday, Ben asked Rina to walk through the park with his art group. chapterReports.title: 節慶卡片
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town festival was near. Morning Corner had a small table on the busy street, and Rina was ready to help. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: walked by the lake and remembered the smile of the boy with the rice cake. The festival had not solved the old problem. chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The weather turned cold, and the shop kitchen felt like a room under a blue sky with no sun. The cook wore two warm coats and asked for a new fan heater. chapterReports.title: 門口的新規則

chapterReports.title: 第一箱新鮮貨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rina's aunt came to Morning Corner with her parents on a bright morning. They owned a small farm and grew fresh lemons. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t always strong," Rina answered. "I needed a lot of help." Her aunt said, "That is how good families work, and good teams too." chapterReports.title: 市場的一餐
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rina went to the market at nine in the morning. She wanted to compare prices for a meal at her shop and a meal at the small restaurant next door. Her sister Mina worked there. Mina wore a green T-shirt and a wide hat. "How is your job?" she asked. "Hard, but good," Rina answered. They looked at tomatoes, beans, and bread. chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: r and the bank page. One question was now very clear: why did the shop pay for a box that never reached its door? chapterReports.title: 花園裡的煙
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rina was in the garden behind Morning Corner when she saw smoke near the kitchen door. She ran inside and found the cook looking at a hot machine. The light was red, and the air smelled strange. "Turn it off," Rina said. The cook did so. They did not try to open the machine. They walked outside, called the repair worker, and kept other people away. The cook was angry because lunch would be late. R
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: felt different now. She was not trying to catch a person because she did not like him. She was learning how to make work safer, one rule at a time. chapterReports.title: 回來的訂單
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mr. Park asked Mark to sit with Rina and June before the store opened. The air was cool, and everyone had a cup of water. Rina put the video time, the food order, and the bank page on the table. "Who placed this order?" she asked. Mark looked at the page. "I did," he said. "Why was it sent to another place?" Rina asked. Mark moved in his seat. "The driver made a mistake," he answered. Rina did not
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: id. "Take June, and let them tell their side." Rina agreed. She thought about how hard it might be to talk to Mark's wife. The woman had her own work and might not know about the orders at all. Rina did not want to make her afraid. She prepared a short list of questions without angry words. Tomorrow she would ask the person who had received the boxes what she had actually seen.

chapterReports.title: 每個人都有發言的位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Today was the day of the meeting. Mr. Park opened the back room and set a large table in the middle. He asked Rina, June, Mark, and the delivery driver to sit. A woman from the river shop also came. Her name was Eva. She was Mark's wife, but she was here as the person who had received the boxes. Rina gave everyone a towel because rain had made the road wet. Then she said, "We need to know where th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ad. "I wanted to ask what you knew." Eva gave a weak smile. "Thank you for that." Outside, the rain had stopped. Rina touched the table once before she left. The room had held many hard words, but it had also held answers. She hoped one day the people from this meeting could look back and say they had been heard. It was a difficult day, but it was a good step toward a fair one.

chapterReports.title: 門邊的訪談
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Another question was still open. Were there any other boxes missing? Mr. Park asked Rina to interview the workers, one by one, with June beside her. The first person was a young man who had joined the shop last year. He said he had seen a black dog near a delivery car once. "I was interested in the dog," he said, "so I did not count the boxes." Rina thanked him. A dog was not proof of anything, bu
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e box had returned. "I cannot answer tonight," she said. "But I will look at the page tomorrow." Rina thanked her. A slow answer from a real page was better than a quick story without proof. She put the phone down and felt tired. She had asked many questions. Now she had to give other people time to do their part. She closed the notebook gently and walked out into the cool air.

chapterReports.title: 線下的那筆錢
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mr. Park came back from a doctor visit with a small smile. The doctor had told him to rest more, but he wanted to see the last bank page. His husband, Ken, came with him and carried the bag. Rina put the page on the table. Below the first total was a second line, written in small letters. It showed money that had been sent out of the shop account for a machine. "What machine?" Mr. Park asked. No o
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: She did not know if she would stay at Morning Corner forever. She knew only that she wanted to work where people could ask honest questions. Outside, the street was quiet. She could hear a dog moving in the yard below her window. Tomorrow would bring work, not a magic answer. That was all right. She had learned that real answers often came from many small days of careful work.

chapterReports.title: 店裡的燈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Tonight Morning Corner was busy, but not with customers. Rina, June, and Mr. Park had come to check the last old orders. They left the front door closed and turned on the little lights over the tables. A piano played softly on the radio. June had worked all day, so Rina asked if she wanted to rest in the back room. "I have enough time for one more page," June said. Then she smiled. "But only one."
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ?" June asked. Rina thought a moment. "Yes. I was afraid to ask a question before. Now I know a question can be a way to care for people." June nodded. They reached the corner and said good night. Rina knew the hard part of the story was not over yet. Mr. Park still had to decide what to do about Mark. But the shop had found its numbers, and that gave everyone a place to begin.

chapterReports.title: 學校的機器人
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A new school program brought students to Morning Corner to learn about shops. One group had made a small robot that could carry a plate across a table. It was only a classroom project, but the children were proud of it. Their teacher asked Rina to explain how workers checked orders. She showed the students a paper card and a computer page. "This is one way to keep the number right," she said. A li
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: king about giving you a new part in the store. We will talk after the final meeting." Rina felt surprised. She did not ask for a promise yet. She wanted to hear the full plan and decide for herself. She put the robot's small thank-you card into her notebook. It showed a bright tiger sitting on a little machine, and the words "Thank you for teaching us" written in large letters.

chapterReports.title: 紙上的名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rina went to the town office with Mr. Park and June. They had come to ask how to keep a clear record of the agreement with Mark. The woman at the desk said hello and asked for their names. Mr. Park gave his name and explained the problem in a polite voice. The woman listened carefully. "I can explain which office can help with a business record," she said, "but I cannot decide your private money p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ce between the clouds, and she could see a few stars. She opened her notebook to the first page. It still held the number that had begun the problem. She had never thought one small note could lead her through the whole town. She closed the book and said yes to one thing: she would keep asking careful questions, wherever she worked next. The shop could change, but so could she.

chapterReports.title: 公平商店遊戲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Morning Corner held a small game for the town on a rainy Saturday. Rina invited friends, workers, and their kids to come. Each person got a paper number and a card with an item to buy. They could choose food from the kitchen or a small gift from the store table. June ran the money box, Ben watched the line, and Leo helped people use a cellphone to see their order. Mr. Park stood nearby but did not
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ave the page to Mr. Park and kept a copy. "Do you want me to put this on the wall?" he asked. "Not the money," Rina said. "Put up the rule. It belongs to everyone." Mr. Park agreed. He wrote the rule in large letters: "Two people check. Everyone can ask. Every change has a record." The words were simple, but they made the room feel new. Rina left with her book and a warm smile.

chapterReports.title: 打烊後，輪到我
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: When the last week of the year came, Morning Corner held a small party. It was not a noisy party. It was a time for the workers and friends to say thank you. Ben made a paper crown for Mr. Park and called him the king of cakes. Mr. Park laughed and gave the crown to a little boy. "I am not a king," he said. "I am a man who needed help." Rina liked that answer. The shop was clean and bright. The fl
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the first morning, when she was afraid to ask about a missing paper. Now she knew when to ask for help, how to check a number, and why every person needed a fair chance to speak. She turned the key and looked at the shop one last time. It did not belong to her, but the work she had done there was hers. Tomorrow she would open the door as manager. Tonight she went home in peace.

chapterReports.title: 空球場
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At seven a.m., Tess heard a bell from the town hall. She was early, but the field was empty. She had a heavy bag with two balls, a notebook, and a cover for the wet grass. The morning sun was bright. Tess was twenty-three years old. She wanted to make a team for a seven-player soccer game. A notice said the town would hold a game in one month, but a team must have seven people. She had only one na
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: balls, took the bag off the couch, and looked at the names once more. Ben wrote the next meeting time at the top of the page. June stood in the door and smiled. Tess had arrived with only her own name on the list. Now Ben had written the next meeting time, and June was still smiling by the door. They did not have seven players yet, but she no longer had to make the plan alone.

chapterReports.title: 七個名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On a sunny afternoon Tess went to the south side of town with Ben. They wanted to find more people for the soccer team. Ben brought his cousin Ava, who could run fast but had never played with a group. Ava had come with her family from a city near a river. She liked to watch science videos and ask why a ball moved in a new direction. Tess told her that asking questions could be helpful on a field.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ide Ava. Ava asked why Tess had not begged Kai to join sooner. "A name is not a promise we can take from someone," Tess answered. "He had to choose." Ava thought about that for a while. She had expected a team to be about a strong kick or a fast run. Now she saw that it could also be about asking, waiting, and listening. The list would stay full only if people wanted to return.

chapterReports.title: 沙地上的線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The seven players could not use the town's best field because another team had it every day after work. Tess looked at a map and found an open place near the beach, not far from a bus station. A narrow road led past a small bridge and into a flat area of sand. A bird was standing beside a pool of water. "Can we play here?" Ava asked. Tess said they should first ask the person who looked after the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: d across the bridge with her notebook. She made two lists. One was about the field: where the water came in and how long they could stay. The other was about the team: who spoke, who waited, and who noticed someone else. She had thought the first practice would show the best player. Instead, it showed her that a safe place and clear words were more important than a strong kick.

chapterReports.title: 小鎮廣場
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Clouds covered the beach on the next practice day. A strong wind began to blow, and Sam said the sand was not safe. Tess did not ask him to change his mind. She took the team back toward town. A worker outside a small factory saw them with their bags. He pointed to a square beside the building. "You can do slow steps there," he said, "if you keep the path open." Tess thanked him and asked whether
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: that one was missing. Leo looked back through the window and saw it by the door. He asked permission to take it. Ms. Park said yes, and he brought it back. The team learned that leaving a borrowed place clean was part of finishing practice. Ava said the square had taught them a strange lesson: sometimes the most useful part of a sports day happened after the ball was put away.

chapterReports.title: 第一次測試
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Tess set a race for the team, but it was not a race to win. Everyone had to run from one point to another, stop, and put a ball beside a bean bag. They could go as slowly as they needed. "Although this looks easy," Tess said, "we must be safe." Rose wanted to try first. She ran a long way and came back in less than one minute. Her neck was red, and she sat down for water. Tess told her she did not
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: with no winner written on the page. Instead, Tess wrote what each person did well: Ben saw the frog, Kai saw the hole, and Rose slowed down for June. The list was not as exciting as a medal, but it showed work they could use in a real match. Before leaving, everyone promised to rest for a full day. A team could learn to run, Tess thought, but it also had to learn when to stop.

chapterReports.title: 名單上的位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The seven players arrived at the town sports house on a weekend morning. A sign at the top of the door said that the soccer game was free, but the team had to put its name on the list before Friday. Inside, a woman sat beside a box of forms and a cup of coffee. She asked Tess to show the seven names. Tess had brought a clean page. She felt as if the small team were stepping into something real for
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: eside her bed. The team now had an official place in the town game, but there was still so much to learn. She remembered how the field manager had listened when Rose spoke. The girl who had once thought that being a leader meant having all the answers now felt differently. A leader could look, ask, and wait. She was ready to do those things again when the team met next weekend.

chapterReports.title: 時間的聲音
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The clock in the park was broken, so the team could not tell when their short practice should end. Tess put a small clock beside the field and asked Leo to watch it. A loud noise from a car made June jump. June told the others that she sometimes found it hard to hear a voice when many people spoke at once. "We can be close enough to see each other," Ava said. "We do not need to shout over the nois
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the park and the quiet in June's yard. Neither place was perfect, but each had taught them a new way to play. She wrote a note: "See the person before you pass." It was simple enough for everyone to remember. She hoped that in the coming game they would have time to look up, even if another team was running toward them. For now, she had learned to hear a friend without a shout.

chapterReports.title: 第一場友誼賽
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The team met another group in the park for a friendly game. On the way, Ben talked about baseball, a game he used to play with his sister. Kai said soccer felt different because the ball had to stay near their feet. Ava wore a blue dress over her shorts because she had come straight from a family meal. She changed behind a screen in the sports house before the game. Rose gave everyone a nice look
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e park together. No one tried to hide the score. They said they had lost one to four and would learn from it. Tess thanked the other players for the friendly game. One of them said, "You are new, but you listen well. Keep going." Tess wrote that line in her notebook. She had wanted to show the town a strong team. Instead, the team had shown her its first small sign of strength.

chapterReports.title: 節慶後的散步
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town festival filled the main street with tables and music. Tess went with her grandmother, who had watched many games in her life. They bought rice and a banana dish, then sat by the lake. Her grandmother said she was ready to hear about the team's first loss. Tess told her the score and added that she was quite sure everyone had tried. "And did you have any joy?" her grandmother asked. Tess
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: her grandmother. There was less noise now, and workers were putting away the festival tables. Her grandmother said that a good coach did not need to speak every minute. Sometimes it was enough to ask a question and give people time to think. Tess looked at the plan in her hand. She had started the team to play soccer. Now she was learning how to make room for six other people.

chapterReports.title: 球網與冰塊
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The sports center opened its field for a short practice. Tess brought a new net, two pencils, and a simple drawing of where players should stand. The center had a teacher who knew soccer, and he agreed to watch for half an hour. "You have five people who can kick well," he said, "but you still need to look between them." Ava loved a quick run, yet today she had to learn when to stop and look to he
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: s they left the center, Kai said his knee felt better, but he would not play again that day. Tess thanked him for making a careful choice. The team did not learn a new way to win in only one afternoon. They did learn how to make room, how to stop when someone fell, and how to listen to a teacher without forgetting their own questions. For Tess, that was enough work for one day.

chapterReports.title: 寒冷天的室內練習
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Cold weather came with a long rain. Tess called the team before anyone left home. She said the field was too wet, so they would meet at the sports center instead. June was in a car with her father when the call came. They turned toward the center and told everyone the road was clear. Rose brought a blue bag of soft balls that would not hurt the walls. "Maybe we can cook something after practice,"
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: at the weather report. It was probably going to rain again, so the next meeting might also be inside. She told everyone that a change of place was not a failure. There were many things they could learn without a large field. Rose stood by the door and said she liked the calm room. The others agreed. For the first time, bad weather had helped them notice the value of slow work.

chapterReports.title: 自己的腳步
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: When spring wind came, the seven players were able to use the field again. Tess arrived on her bicycle and found a small bow tied to the gate. It was a welcome from the field manager. She picked a safe place for their bags, then called everyone together. "Today each of you will choose your own next step," she said. "I can give you an idea, but the choice is yours." Ben said he wished he could lear
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: a wish of her own. She wanted each player to feel that this team was partly theirs. "I may have started it," she said, "but I do not own it." The others thought about that for a moment. Kai said he would be glad to lead the next warm-up if people wanted him to. They agreed, and Tess wrote his name beside the next date. She had given away a small task and gained a stronger team.

chapterReports.title: 鎖住的大門
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The team came to the city field one morning and found the gate closed. A paper notice said that another group had borrowed the field for the day. Tess checked the date. It was the same day they had booked, and their own name was on the schedule in her phone. Ben began to feel angry. He said someone had broken a rule. Tess asked him to stand with the others while she found the person in charge. She
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e, Tess remembered the first time she had played soccer as a small child. She had thought the world was simple: someone said yes or no, and that was all. Now she knew that two people could both have a good reason for using the same place. A fair answer did not mean making one group feel small. She sent the new booking time to everyone and asked them to check it before tomorrow.

chapterReports.title: 守門員的手套
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Rose arrived with a new pair of gloves. Her aunt had given them to her after hearing about the team. "I can catch the ball better with these," Rose said. Her aunt had run a small business for many years and knew that money was not always easy to find. She had bought the gloves during a sale, not because they were beautiful, but because they fit Rose's hands. Tess asked her to check the size before
