chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ose took off her gloves and placed them in her bag. She said she felt ready for the next match, but she wanted to learn more before calling herself a good goalkeeper. Tess said that was a strong choice. She did not have to prove everything today. The team walked out through the gate together, and Rose stayed behind for one moment to help the boy return his soft ball to its box.

chapterReports.title: 一件球衣的價格
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The team needed shirts in the same color for the town game. Ava went to the market and found a shop with a bright blue T-shirt, but it was expensive. Ben had a job at a restaurant and knew how much one shirt could cost a person who worked by the hour. "How can we make this fair?" he asked. Tess said no one should have to give up a meal or use money they needed for something else just to be on the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: That night Tess counted the cost again. They needed no new shirts, no big meal, and no special machine. What they did need was time to wash the shirts and check that the colors were clear. She sent the new plan to everyone. No one had to pay money to keep a place on the team. She felt happy when six short replies came back, each with the same answer: "Yes, this works for me."

chapterReports.title: 炎熱的球場
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The heat came early that week. Tess looked at the sky and said the air was too hot for a fast game at noon. She made a new plan: a short practice in the morning, with water breaks under the trees. Kai looked angry because he wanted more time on the field. "We are strong enough," he said. Tess shook her head. "Being strong also means knowing when to stop." June agreed and brought a little tea for l
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: , Kai walked with Tess and said he had been wrong to ask for a longer practice. He had seen Ben resting, and he now understood that not everyone had the same day at work. Tess said she too sometimes wanted to push too hard. She was learning that a leader did not have to win every talk. They could make a correct choice together, even if that choice was to stop and go home early.

chapterReports.title: 凱為什麼回來
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Kai missed the next meeting. Tess called him once, but he did not answer. She did not send many messages. The team had enough people for a light practice, and Kai had a right to his own time. Two days later, he came to the field with a worried face. "I could not decide if I wanted to play again," he said. "At work I feel tired, and I do not have enough air after a long day." Tess asked if he wante
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ai said he was grateful no one had made him feel bad for staying away. Tess answered that the team needed people, not just names on a sheet. They both knew the coming game would be hard. They also knew they could face it in different ways. Some people would run, some would rest, and some would help from the side. Kai had returned because there was room for all of those choices.

chapterReports.title: 瓊帶領的一天
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Today June was the leader. Tess gave her the team notebook and said she could set the practice as she thought best. June was nervous because she did not like giving orders, but she had a good plan. She asked everyone to stand on the grass in two small groups. Her father, Mr. Chen, came to watch from the side with his younger child. He told June that she did not need to be loud to be clear. She smi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: up, June gave the notebook back to Tess. Tess told her to keep it until the next meeting because she wanted June to write her own notes. June said she would. She had always thought a leader needed to speak first and make everyone listen. Today she had made space for many voices. Tess walked home with an empty hand where the notebook had been. It felt strange, but it felt right.

chapterReports.title: 球門旁的蜜蜂
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first town game was held on a bright morning. Tess and her team wore blue shirts with seven small marks in a circle. Before the game began, a bee flew near the goal. Rose stepped away slowly, and an officer asked everyone to wait. A dog on the path barked at the ball but stayed with its owner. The game would start only when the field was clear. Tess counted seven players, then checked that the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: Tess what the most important moment had been. Tess did not say it was the goal. She told him about Rose stopping when a player fell, and about June finding an open place. "I am interested in how we play," she said, "not only what number is on the board." The reporter wrote her words down. Tess looked at the seven marks on her shirt and thought they finally meant something real.

chapterReports.title: 再拿一分
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next game was against a strong team from another town. Tess had heard about them from a friend abroad, but she knew a story from far away did not tell her how they would play today. She asked everyone to focus on their own part. Before the game, Ben had eggs and bread with butter. Kai said he could not eat much because he was nervous. June told him to take his time. The team had a simple goal:
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the game. He listened while she told him about the noise, the grass, and the goal. Dan said he was proud of her, but he did not ask why the team had not won. "You are doing your part," he said. Tess thought about her friends, who all did their own part too. She felt tired, but the tired feeling was good. Their story was not over, and she did not need to know the ending tonight.

chapterReports.title: 今晚的一盞燈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town put the game results on a board by the sports center door. Tess and the team went there after work. They were busy people, and this was the only time all seven could meet that day. The board showed they had two points, with one game left to play. A small light over the page made the words easy to read. Tess felt nervous, but she did not try to hide it. "We have one more chance," she said,
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ss the dark sky toward the airport. Leo pointed up, then looked back at the team. "People go to many places," he said, "but tonight I am glad to be here." Tess nodded. She had spent weeks asking other people to join her dream. Now her friends were choosing to stay, not because she needed them to, but because they wanted to be there. She turned off the field light and went home.

chapterReports.title: 長椅上的老虎
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Friday, the team went to the park for a short walk. They did not want to use all their strength before Saturday's game. Near a bench, a baby was sleeping in a chair, with a toy tiger beside it. A little boy was trying to make a robot from paper boxes. He asked the players if they would help him carry it down the path. Tess said they could help after they checked that the way was dry and safe. T
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ort path home. They had walked only a little way, but Tess felt rested. No one had tried to turn the quiet day into another hard practice. They had helped a child and learned from him too. When Tess checked her bag, her shoes were dry and her notebook was safe. Tomorrow there would be a real game with a score. Today had been about moving slowly and seeing the world around them.

chapterReports.title: 辦公室裡的比分
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Saturday morning, the team came to the sports office to check the new game table. The woman behind the desk said hello and asked for their team name. Tess gave it to her and waited politely. The table showed one team with seven points, another with four, and Tess's team with two. There was still one game for her team. If they won, they could reach five points and play in the final. If they lost
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: cked the field and said the afternoon game could go ahead. Tess looked at the table one last time and wrote the numbers in her notebook. This time she understood them. She did not know whether they would make the final, but the way was clear. They needed to win the last group game, and they needed to play it with care. She put the notebook away and joined her friends for lunch.

chapterReports.title: 雨後的比賽
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The last group game began after a light rain. The ground was wet, but the manager had checked it and said it was safe. Tess met the other team's leader near the gate. He told her his players were ready. They had both been invited to the same game and wanted to play their best. Tess used her cellphone to send the final time to a friend who was on the way. Then she put it away. There would be no nee
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e points and reached the final. Tess checked the official number before telling everyone. Then she hugged her friends one by one. They were tired, wet, and happy. The other team shook hands with them and wished them well. On the way home, Tess listened to the radio in Ben's uncle's car. The sports report said their team had moved to the final. It was a sound she would remember.

chapterReports.title: 最後一聲哨響
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the morning of the final, Tess woke up before the sun was high. Her husband Dan had to go to the airport to meet his boss, but he promised to come to the game when he could. Tess made a simple plan for breakfast and cut fruit into small pieces. She did not feel like a king or a great sports star. She felt like a regular person about to do something hard with six friends. The sight of her blue s
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: They ate food they had prepared, thanked the people who had helped, and made a plan for next season. Tess said she would like to play again, but each person could choose. One by one, six friends said yes. Dan came to stand beside Tess as the sky grew dark. The game was over, but their team was not. Tess closed the notebook at last, happy to know when the next page would begin.

chapterReports.title: 沒有鳥鳴的早晨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In Cloudpine Valley, winter did not end on the same day every year. Tavi, a young red panda, woke before the sun. A small bug crept along the cold window. Tavi wondered why it had appeared so early. She opened the window and listened for the birds that usually returned before spring, but heard none. Her camera hung beside the door. She took a picture of the white hills, yet a picture could not sho
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ped her ask a better question. Ivo returned to check that she had eaten. Nell brought a spare pencil and reminded her to rest. Tavi was grateful. She could look for the spring sounds without turning every hour into work. Before going to bed, she wrote, “We may hear something tomorrow, or we may hear nothing new. Both days can teach us.” The line made her feel ready for morning.

chapterReports.title: 暖石旁的會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The friends met at Nell's apartment, a small home cut into a warm hillside. Anybody could come to the meeting, so a few neighbors sat on flat stones by the door. Nell began by asking them not to guess about the weather. An old church stood across the valley, but its road was too icy today. “We can stay here,” she said. “The ground is clear, and we can hear each other.” A visiting reporter had come
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t only the day before. She thought of the families who might read their report. They would need clear words and real dates, not a brave-sounding story. Ivo waited outside and kept the path free for the older deer. When all three friends reached home, they sent a short note to the others. Tomorrow's walk would begin only after the morning check. Everyone now knew what to expect.

chapterReports.title: 冰下的水聲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: All the paths near the lower pond looked white, but Nell knew the area well. She told Tavi to begin at a tree with three low branches. Two young goats were playing basketball near their home. Their ball made a loud sound against a wall. Tavi laughed, then stopped to define the sound they wanted to hear: not every noise was a sign of spring. Ivo asked the goats to keep playing; this search was not
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e not finished yet. When a question stayed open, they had a reason to return with care and compare days. Tavi looked at the pale picture on her camera. It showed the pond, the dry path, and the far trees. It did not show the soft sound. That was why she needed words as well as pictures. She closed the book before dinner, knowing that a good search could leave room for tomorrow.

chapterReports.title: 走錯的綠色道路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next day, the three friends met by an outdoor bath fed by warm mountain water. A large block of snow lay on the path beyond it. Both Nell and Ivo knew they had a choice: turn around or cross the open field to the east. The field looked green where the wind had moved the snow, but that did not make it safe. Tavi shook her head when a young animal wanted to run across. “We must not pass a place
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ed him to explain why it could be soft too. They spoke with the driver before he began his next trip. The driver repeated the warning in his own words so they knew he understood. Tavi felt relieved. The day's best discovery was not a new sound; it was learning that a short path could hide a long risk. Their careful choice gave the next visitors a better chance to travel safely.

chapterReports.title: 月亮路的農場
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the next safe day, the friends visited a small farm near a bend called Moon Road. A bank office had helped the farmer buy a new water tank, and he was proud of caring for his animals without waste. He had to feed many hungry mouths before sunrise. A letter from his sister lay on the table, beside a cup of milk. Outside, the moon was still bright. Tavi had come to ask about the birds that once s
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: line to their method: ask what changed around the sound. Ivo remembered his sore toe and laughed when he stepped around the same stone on their next visit. The group thanked the family for showing them real work and real care. Tavi also promised not to bring visitors into the farm without asking first. It was a home and a place of work, not an open field for everyone to enter.

chapterReports.title: 泥地旁的座位
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A warmer day brought good news from the lower stream. Nell set a desk by her window and spread their notes across it. The deep snow near the bank had changed to soft mud. “Do we go now?” Ivo asked, lifting one arm. Tavi wanted to find the answer, but the soft ground could be unsafe. They decided to visit the public rest place first. It had a convenient seat and a roof where they could wait without
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: lp clean the rest place once a week. Tavi liked the idea because it gave the neighbors something useful to do without pushing closer to the river. They made a small plan to ask the town who would care for the seat. It was a simple job, but it would help many people watch the changing season. Tavi felt that their search was slowly becoming a shared way of living with the valley.

chapterReports.title: 草地上的課
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: By the next week, children were asking about the search. A local teacher offered a short class in a dry meadow beside the west road. She told Tavi that learning by listening could be useful, but the class must stay by the main path. Tavi agreed. The teacher gave each child a list of safe things to hear: wind, water, feet, and leaves. “We collect notes, not animals,” she said. A young rabbit brough
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the place where he stood. Another child had drawn a bird, even though she had heard only leaves. She decided to draw the leaves instead and save the bird for another day. No one was scolded for changing a page. The whole class understood that careful notes could become better with a second look. Tavi went home carrying many little pictures and a new respect for young listeners.

chapterReports.title: 收藏舊聲音的房間
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The local museum had a small room for old sounds. Tavi borrowed a book about the valley and went there with Nell. The trip was not dangerous, and the museum stood near a train stop. Each visitor paid one dollar to help keep the room clean. The guide said anyone who could not pay could enter free. Tavi liked that idea. A visit was successful when a person learned something, not when the museum sold
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: boy, “and you may notice something new.” Tavi agreed. They did not need to take the recording home or call it a living bird. The boy looked through the old pictures one final time before leaving. Tavi felt that the day had given him a better way to use his curiosity. She thanked the guide for letting questions be part of the visit rather than rushing everyone from room to room.

chapterReports.title: 聽不見鳥聲的熊
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A bear named Alden lived alone near the upper farms. He was brave on the mountain, but he had become lonely after his sister moved far away. A farmer told Tavi that Alden once knew every bird in the valley. They went to ask for his help, taking no meat or milk for wild animals along the way. They carried only their own food. Alden opened his door with a sad look. He had not heard birds for some ti
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: promised to bring a clean sheet next week. Ivo suggested that Alden also write about the days when nothing new happened. The bear thought for a moment and agreed. He had often felt ashamed of quiet days. Now he could see that a quiet day was not an empty one. He thanked his new friends and opened his window just a little, letting the cool air in without stepping into the snow.

chapterReports.title: 風說現在還不能走
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Dark clouds moved around the western hills one evening. Tavi had a button missing from her coat, but she did not go outside to look for it. The sky was changing fast. Some leaves began to fall from the trees, and the wind carried them past her window. She had a little menu of hot food on the table because Nell was coming for dinner. There were potatoes and a sweet cake. Tavi found the sound of lea
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: had reached home, and Ivo said the town had closed the high road. Tavi wrote these facts beside the weather notes. After that, she put her book away. The wind outside still sounded strong, but there was no work she needed to do in the dark. Rest was part of staying ready. She went to sleep knowing that the morning could bring a new plan, and she would be able to change with it.

chapterReports.title: 薄冰的規則
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: In the morning, Tavi carried a basket of food to the small hospital. The storm had left several paths wet, and a young kite maker had slipped near the river. His health was good, but his leg needed rest. The nurse checked him and told his mother what to watch for. Tavi brought no big plan to the hospital; she came to help carry dry clothes. She thought it useful to hear how a careful adult made a
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: one clear picture. Ivo offered to send the same information to the families who had asked about the stream. He would not send a private patient's story or name. Tavi thanked him for remembering that safety information could be shared without sharing personal details. The next time they heard a bird by the hospital, they would still begin by checking the ground under their feet.

chapterReports.title: 全鎮決定聆聽
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On a clear afternoon, the town met near the supermarket to hear news about the search. An actor from a visiting group offered to read Tavi's notes, but Tavi said she wanted to speak in her own voice. “I can do it,” she said. She put on her glasses and held the key to the meeting room. A small band was practicing at the next corner, so they asked the players to wait until the talk ended. They did n
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: high hill. Ivo put the clean copy in a folder where anyone could read it. The friends understood that a public talk was not the end of their work. The words on the page might guide visitors days later, after the weather had changed. That was why dates and warnings mattered. Tavi felt nervous about being wrong, yet she knew she could correct a note when better evidence arrived.

chapterReports.title: 棕色鴨子的路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The friends went to a beautiful valley camp where the hill was high but the main road was wide and dry. A brown duck named Hedi lived there with her family. She set a chair beside a window and gave everyone warm tea with a little honey. Though the sky looked bright, a line of rain stood over the far peaks. Hedi told them not to ride up the narrow hill that day. She was a member of the local safety
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: tones without moving away from the porch. Nell asked the others what they had learned. Each friend gave a different answer, and the soldier said those answers could all be useful. They had learned about rain, about waiting, and about keeping a group together. Tavi added one last line to her notes: a safe camp is still part of the mountain, and listening there is real listening.

chapterReports.title: 診所的一張紙
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: One morning an ant walked across Tavi's bag while she sat in the clinic waiting room. A clerk was helping an older chicken find a seat. The chicken had a small hurt foot and was carrying a bottle of water. The doctor said she was not seriously sick, but she should rest and try a shoe of the right size. Tavi offered her own chair. The clerk hung the chicken's wet coat by the door. Several neighbors
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he doctor looked at the note and said the idea was kind. But she also reminded them that an activity was not a treatment for illness. People who needed care should still ask their health workers for help. Tavi wrote that down. She did not want to call a pleasant moment a cure. Making room for someone was a good thing by itself, without a promise that it could fix every problem.

chapterReports.title: 草上方的小小叫聲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning was lovely. A few clouds moved above the valley, and the sun made the snow bright. Tavi had a chance to join the clinic's short listening visit. She could choose to run ahead to the meadow, but she decided to walk beside an older guest instead. The guest was with her daughter and carried a small gift of warm tea in her pocket. Tavi told them that no gift was needed. Their pleasure
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: call to make the visit complete. Later, Tavi compared the notes from the different listeners and found that they agreed about the short call, even if their counts were different. She wrote down both the agreement and the difference. That was more useful than choosing just one person's memory. The moment had been lovely, and a careful record would help them learn from it again.

chapterReports.title: 灰樹間的風
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The day was bright, but a change had come to the forest. The gray trees beside the path made a low sound when the wind passed between their branches. Tavi went with Nell to visit a grandfather pig who knew the land well. He had a habit of sitting beside the same tree each morning, with a small pink cup in his hand. “The tree is not singing to us,” he said. “It is moving in the wind.” Tavi asked fo
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: yed hearing about his life but did not write the old sea sound as something found in Cloudpine Valley. She made a small note about his memory instead. Nell said the difference mattered because readers might otherwise think the sea was just beyond the hill. The old pig laughed and agreed. A story could travel far, but a map still needed to tell the truth about where things were.

chapterReports.title: 聆聽者的圓圈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A friend from the town asked Tavi to help build a small circle of seats near the rest place. It would be the best spot for people who wanted to listen while sitting. Everything had to stay on dry ground, away from the stream. Nell drew a circle with her hand in the air and showed how chairs could face different ways. Ivo brought an old drum to test whether the place carried loud sound. Tavi asked
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ats without running across wet grass. The friends looked at the dry path and agreed to keep it open. They would not put more chairs in the way. Tavi learned that the best design was not always the one with the most things. It was the one people could use safely, with room to move and to choose where they wanted to sit. She promised to ask the visitors again after the next rain.

chapterReports.title: 折返的巴士
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Tavi went along the main road with Nell to visit a safe viewing place near the zoo. Their bus carried a dozen visitors, and the driver gave everyone time to sit before moving. Tavi had brought bread for dinner and a toy made of wood for a child at the zoo office. The weather looked excellent, but the driver warned that one sharp turn could be bad after rain. He checked the road before leaving town
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: r explaining. The children now understood that care was not just a feeling; it meant doing real work before moving. Back in town, Tavi asked the bus office to share the closure notice with other drivers. The office agreed. She was glad she could help without telling anyone to take an unknown side road. The group had seen how a safe turn back could protect a whole bus of people.

chapterReports.title: 不是每個聲音都是魔法
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At home, Tavi set a cup of cool water beside her bed and looked at the notes she had made. She wanted to become a better listener, but she was beginning to see that practice took time. A school teacher had asked her to visit a class and show children how to make a short sound list. She decided to carry only a small bag, not a computer or many heavy things. Nell tied the bag shut with a strong stri
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ry the listening game at home with family members. They could start at a safe window or a garden path. Nobody needed to climb a hill to practice. Tavi felt happy that a difficult idea could become a simple rule without losing its meaning. Tavi was proud that every child could join the lesson in a way that felt safe. Some spoke, some drew, and others preferred to listen quietly.

chapterReports.title: 帶小提琴的訪客
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: One morning, an elephant appeared in the town square with a small violin case. He was a traveler from a warmer place and wanted to see the mountain snow before it was gone. Everyone thought the visit was exciting, but he warned that a beautiful sound could fail if the player did not practice. “I am no fool,” he said with a smile, “and I will not play while my hands are cold and wet.” He had carrie
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: . Nobody wanted the musician to fail or feel ashamed; they simply respected his choice not to play in the wet air. Nell wrote a short thank-you note about the visit. She said that music made by people and sounds made by nature could both give joy without becoming the same thing. Tavi agreed. The valley had room for many kinds of listening, as long as each was treated with care.

chapterReports.title: 每個人的聆聽位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A local walking club held a meeting to talk about the future of the sound route. Tavi had always wanted a good place where young and old neighbors could learn together. But she knew every new sign had a cost, and somebody would have to do the work of caring for it. The club leader played a short guitar tune to open the holiday meeting, then put the guitar away. “We will listen to one another now,”
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: rs to sort through. A young member said she would help read the notices to anyone who wanted that. Nell thanked her and added her name to the shared list. Tavi thought about how many different skills were now part of the work. Some people listened to birds, some checked paths, and some helped neighbors understand words. They were learning to take care of a whole place together.

chapterReports.title: 工程師與舊故事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: An engineer visited the town to check the small public rest place. She had the ability to see problems that others might miss. She studied the floor, the glass windows, and the path outside. She told Tavi that she would draw a simple plan before making any changes. A lot of new things were not needed. The old chairs were still good, and the building was not dead or beyond use. One door needed a be
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: heck the space. Nell added it to the meeting notes. They had learned to make requests without demanding answers on the spot. A good plan needed listening from both sides: people who knew how to build and people who knew what they needed to use. The friends decided to place a chair near each open window so visitors could choose what felt right. Nobody had to sit in only one way.

chapterReports.title: 厚草裡的蛇
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Tavi and Nell went to study the grass near the warm rocks, with Ivo walking behind them. A small snake lay in the thick grass, warming itself in the sun. Tavi stopped at once. She told the group not to move closer or try to kill the snake. The animal was at home, and the visitors could choose another way. Ivo raised his hand to mark a safe stopping place. “No,” he said firmly when a child wanted t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ild area next to it should not be entered. Tavi wrote both facts down. She was beginning to see that a careful note could hold a yes and a no at the same time. The world was rarely as simple as one big green mark or one big red mark. From the dry path, the children could still hear the insects. That was all they needed for the day, and they went home without touching the grass.

chapterReports.title: 不屬於我們的池塘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The friends almost missed the first warm afternoon by staying indoors to finish notes. Tavi put on a light jacket, and Nell took a carrot for her own lunch. They were careful about the little hill beside the pond, because the rain had made one foot path soft. They did not buy new shoes or take a boat. The safe bank was enough. A row of stones kept visitors away from the water. Tavi was glad the to
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: for our list.” Nell smiled and agreed. They also decided not to tell visitors to come at night to seek the calls. The bank had not been checked for night visits, and darkness could make the ground harder to see. Tavi was content with the afternoon record. The frogs could call when they wanted, and people could learn about them without standing beside their homes at every hour.

chapterReports.title: 七種聲音，同一座山谷
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: By the end of spring, Tavi was able to read her whole notebook without feeling afraid of the blank places. She had learned to allow some questions to remain open. Her cat slept in a comfortable chair beside a small doll, while Nell and Ivo came for the final meeting. Tavi had made a map of seven listening places. It did not tell visitors that every sound would happen at the same time. It showed sa
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e ways to listen, not a test that each person had to finish. The listeners were free to take part in one safe part or several. When the room grew quiet, Alden thanked Tavi for teaching him to trust his ears again. She answered that he had helped her just as much. The search had started with one person at one window; it ended with many neighbors taking care of one living valley.

chapterReports.title: 山上的鈴聲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At six a.m., Erin opened her eyes. She was twenty-four and had come to Hill Village only yesterday. The sun was not high yet, but a little bell rang outside her window. She got up early because she wanted to see the old blue windmill on the hill. It was her first day in the village, and she did not want to be late. Her room was small. There was a bed, a table, and a green couch. On the table was a
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: lp us.” Erin answered, “I want to learn what happened. Then we can talk about what to do.” The old man smiled. “Good. Shall we begin with the story of this hill?” He rang the bell once, softly. Erin opened her book to a clean page. Under the words First Day, she wrote one question: Why did the blue windmill stop? She did not know the answer yet, but now she knew where to begin.

chapterReports.title: 小小數字的紀錄
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next morning Erin returned to Mrs. May's kitchen with a question: how much power had the windmill really made? Mrs. May said the answer was in a book at the village room. Ben offered to bring Erin there. His cousin Mira was also visiting that day. Mira worked at a science center in the south, where she showed children how simple machines worked. "A famous building can still have a small job,"
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: . "We do not know why it stopped, or what it would cost to make it safe. Those are our next questions." Mrs. May looked at the drawings. "Then we must not ask a family to pay for a promise," she said. "Let us learn the cost first." They agreed to visit the old river path the next day, but only from the public road. Erin wrote that rule in her notebook so nobody would forget it.

chapterReports.title: 河邊的那條線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The old road followed the river before it turned toward the hill. Erin, Mira, and Ben stopped beside a small bridge. Below it, the water moved between round stones. There was a narrow beach of pale sand on one side. A black bird stood there, watching the water. "The old water line crossed this bridge," Mr. Han said. He had come to show them the way. "I was born here, so I remember when the pipe wa
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ce. A plan for one would change work at the others. Mrs. May asked whether the walk had been useful. Erin said it had been useful because they had found things they should not touch. "A good worker knows when to stop," Mrs. May said. Erin smiled and put her pencil down. Tomorrow she would ask the town office who was responsible for the closed windmill, and who could inspect it.

chapterReports.title: 看似容易的提議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Monday, a tall worker from the old furniture factory came to the town office. His name was Paul. He carried a square box of blue paint and said the factory could give it to the village for a cheap price. "The wind will blow soon," he said. "Why not put on fresh paint and open the hill?" A boy near the door liked that idea. He told a story about a butterfly sitting on the windmill years ago. Eri
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ted to the three steps on the wall. "We all want a good town," she said. "That means asking questions before we spend money." The man read the list again and said nothing more. Erin went outside with her notebook. It was not a win or a loss. It was one useful rule that people could read for themselves. Tomorrow, she would look for a safe way to measure the wind from the ground.

chapterReports.title: 不必比誰先登頂
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A thin layer of snow fell during the night, even though it was almost spring. In the morning, Ben wanted to race Erin to the top of the hill. "At least let me win once," he said. His long scarf moved in the wind. Erin pointed to a wet sign near the path. "No race today. The ground is not safe." Ben looked sorry. Mr. Han came out of his house and showed them a better place to stand. The path near t
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: "A long job must be done one piece at a time," she said. Mr. Han agreed and told them about a day many years ago when a man had tried to work in bad weather. Everyone had asked him to stop, and he had listened. That choice had kept the team safe. Ben wrote the story beneath his drawing. He did not feel like a loser anymore. He was glad his map might help someone else next week.

chapterReports.title: 週末的會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: By the weekend, news about the windmill had reached every house. Some people arrived at the village room by car; others came on foot. A man from the lake district had driven a small boat across the water before taking a bus into town. He carried a box of old photographs. Mrs. May offered coffee, and Erin put a paper sign on the door: Please speak one at a time. The meeting was free and open to eve
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: t hill, and the people she had met. "I would rather stay and see what we learn," she answered. "But I can take a day off if I need one." Mrs. May smiled. "Good. A person is not a machine." Erin put the meeting paper in her notebook and closed it. She would wait for the inspection results instead of guessing. The bell rang once in the distance, a soft sound across the dark town.

chapterReports.title: 等待的聲音
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The day after the meeting was quiet. Erin woke in her bedroom and looked at the clock. The windmill was still closed, and she could not make the inspection happen sooner. Mrs. May had left a note in the yard: Good work takes time. Erin read it twice. She believed that, but she did not like waiting. Ben came over with a drawing of a rainbow above the hill. "I had a dream that the arms were turning,
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: mall clock. She could not know whether tomorrow would bring rain or sunshine, or whether the inspector would find good news. She could choose how to use the time before then. She made a copy of her notes for Nora and left it in the town office. On the way back, the bell sounded over the yard. Erin looked at the dark hill and felt ready to hear whatever the inspection would say.

chapterReports.title: 檢查員看見的事
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ms. Patel arrived with another inspector on a clear morning. Erin and a small group waited outside the fence. The inspectors wore work clothes, strong shoes, and safety hats. They checked the outside first, then entered the windmill through a door kept closed to visitors. Ben could not see what happened behind the wall, and he asked why the children had to stay in the park below. "An officer who c
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ven while the tower remains closed," she said. June thought of making paper arms that would turn in a gentle breeze. Ben suggested a small stand to hold drawings. The children began talking about shapes and colors. Erin did not tell them to stop. An old building could not be made safe by wishing, but a good lesson could begin with paper, a pencil, and people willing to ask why.

chapterReports.title: 小點子的節日
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The town was preparing for its spring festival near the lake. This year, Nora offered the village room one long table. "You may show what you have learned about the windmill," she said. "But no one may visit the tower yet." Erin agreed. Ben made a card with a picture of the old blue arms, and June brought a dish of rice to share at lunch. Her grandmother came with her and told everyone how she had
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: one person," she told him. "There is no magic dish that everyone must like." Ben laughed and put the cards in three neat piles. The group would treat every note with care, even notes they did not agree with. On the walk home, Erin felt tired but hopeful. The festival had not fixed a single piece of wood. It had given the project something else: more voices and better questions.

chapterReports.title: 中間的那塊地方
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Two days later, a music teacher named Ada came to see the festival cards. Ada was blind, and she used a white cane to find her way. Her brother walked beside her but let her choose where to go. "I love hearing the hill bell," Ada said. "I do not need to stand right next to the tower. I need a safe way to reach a good listening place." Erin showed her the map and the Little Lookout between the gard
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: head. "Good friends can tell you a hard truth. That is one way to show love." Erin wrote this sentence beside the map. She did not know whether the town would pay for a whole new path, but she knew that a listening space could not be called ready while someone was stopped by a loose stone. They would bring the idea to the next meeting, with a clear picture and no easy promises.

chapterReports.title: 寒天裡的藍色資料夾
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The weather turned cold, and a hard wind moved through the trees. Nora called Erin from her car. "The inspector's full report is ready," she said. "Come to the town office before the snow starts." Erin put on warm pants and took the blue folder she had used for her notes. Mrs. May, who liked to cook soup on cold days, packed a small bowl for her. "You may be there for a long time," she said. In th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e a real plan. She drew three columns: work that must happen, work that might happen, and ideas that could wait. The roof and brake went into the first column. A learning model went into the second. A bright new coat of blue paint went into the third. Mrs. May brought warm soup. "A plan can be changed when we learn more," she said. Erin folded the pages and felt warmer already.

chapterReports.title: 小小測風實驗
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the first warm day of spring, Mira came by bicycle with a paper wind wheel in her bag. She wore old jeans and carried a notebook of her own. "This is a model for the Little Lookout," she said. "It does not need anyone to touch the real windmill." Ben wanted to pick it up right away, but Mira asked him to wait. "First answer one question: what will make it turn?" "The wind," Ben said. Mira gave
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: le could learn without entering the tower. She was surprised that the second page now held more ideas than the first. There were ways to see, hear, touch safe models, and ask questions. She chose three ideas to bring to Nora. Then she closed the book. The wind outside the window was gentle. It had not promised anything, and Erin was finally learning not to ask it for a promise.

chapterReports.title: 打開大門的代價
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next week, Nora invited everyone to a public meeting at the small hotel beside the town gate. The village room was too small for so many people. Erin came in her old coat and stood beside the board with the inspector's report. "The town has a rule," Nora said. "We show costs before we ask people to agree." Erin felt her stomach turn. She was young, and she had never spoken to such a big group
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the path after it was built? A new path could be useful for one year, then become unsafe if no one cleaned it. She added that question to the list. Mrs. May brought a pot of warm water for tea and sat with her. "A good plan has room for tomorrow's work," she said. Erin wrote a new line: Care after opening. It was small, but it changed how she would speak at the final town vote.

chapterReports.title: 第一次同意
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The cost sheet had been on the town office wall for a week. On Friday, Nora called a public vote. Ben came with his aunt, who worked at a small business near the market. She wore a green uniform and carried a bag of fresh lemons for the meeting table. "I can help with food," she said, "but I cannot pay for a new machine." Erin told her that nobody had to give money. The first question was not abou
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ow. "Did you get your answer?" Mrs. May asked. "We got one answer," Erin said. "We can begin the safe work. We still have much to learn." Mrs. May squeezed a lemon into two glasses of water and gave one to her. They sat on the steps as the light grew soft. Erin remembered her father's rule: measure first, cut later. The village had made a careful first cut in a very large plan.

chapterReports.title: 把事情做好要花多少錢
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first prices came back higher than Erin had hoped. A safe roof repair would be expensive, and the path needed more work than a quick look had shown. At breakfast, Erin sat with a sore head and a cold meal. "How can we do both jobs?" she asked. Mrs. May, wearing a wide hat for the garden, told her to eat before worrying again. "The town has made a choice," she said. "Now it can look for a sensi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: job, done safely and honestly. She thought of how many people had given time instead of money. Ben had drawn maps. Ada had tested the path. Mr. Han had shared his memories. Mira had corrected the old numbers. None of that work appeared as a sale on the market sheet, but it mattered. Erin put the note beside the cost table. She felt ready to show it to everyone the next morning.

chapterReports.title: 菜園裡炎熱的一天
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A warm week came quickly. The earth by the garden was dry, and the heat made the workers take more breaks. Erin went to watch the path team, not to tell them how to move their machines. She wore a hat and carried tea and water. A worker showed her the correct line for the new path. "We keep the path away from the old pipe," he said. "That way, we do not make a new problem while fixing an old one."
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: me parts were ready; other parts still needed work. Erin copied the list into her notebook and asked whether any children had been inside the work area. "No," the leader said. "The fence and signs helped." Erin felt that one promise had been kept. They could work with the land and still look after people. On the way home, she saw the first small flowers opening beside the road.

chapterReports.title: 風能告訴我們什麼
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Mira came with a small wind meter that measured moving air. She asked Nora for permission to make observations at the Little Lookout, far from the old machine. Ben watched her place the meter at a safe height. "Is the wind strong enough to turn the arms?" he asked. "That is not the right question yet," Mira answered. "Even with enough wind, the arms must stay still until a repair team has done its
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ildren might see that the weather changes." Erin agreed, but wanted one sentence under the picture: Wind speed is not a safety test for the old tower. Mira wrote it neatly. The reason for the note was simple. A picture could teach a true idea, but it could also make people think something that was not true. They wanted to teach carefully, just as they wanted to build carefully.

chapterReports.title: 山坡上的一支隊伍
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the day before the spring school visit, Mr. Han asked the children to help prepare the village room. "Today we make an indoor lesson," he said. "Tomorrow the trained workers will be at the tower, so the hill will stay closed." Ben's father carried in a giant paper picture of the windmill. Ms. Cho set out chairs, and Nora checked the open door. A younger child wanted to jump from a bench onto th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: for today. A safe fence, a clear lesson, and a team that listened were better than an early show. Ms. Cho thanked her before leaving. "Children remember what adults do more than what adults say," she said. Erin hoped Ben would remember the quiet work as well as the bright pictures. She turned out the lights and closed the door gently, ready for tomorrow's repair work to begin.

chapterReports.title: 圍欄旁的蜜蜂
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The repair team had just arrived when Ben saw a bee moving close to the new path. Then he saw another, and another. A small group had made a home in an old wooden box near the fence. "Will they attack us?" he asked. The garden keeper, who knew the animals around the hill, told him not to wave his arms or try to move the box. "A bee may bite or sting if it feels threatened," he explained. "Stand ba
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: the team had found another way to join the path to the lookout. "A year ago, I might have been angry at losing a day," Erin said to Mrs. May. "Now I think we gained something." Mrs. May looked up from her sewing. "What was that?" she asked. "A better plan," Erin answered. From the open window they could hear a quiet sound in the garden. The hill was home to more than one story.

chapterReports.title: 台階下的水
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: After a night of rain, the path team found water below the new steps. It was not a deep pool, but it was enough to make the ground soft. The team leader stopped work and asked Nora to come. Erin stood in front of the fence, looking at the wet place. "Is anything broken?" she asked. The leader pointed to a low stone wall. "There may be an old part of the water system under here. We will need to che
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: abroad on roads visited the site and offered advice. Nora thanked him but asked the hired team to check it against the local plan. "Experience is useful," she said, "and responsibility must be clear." Erin added the new line to her map. The windmill still stood quiet above the hill. For the first time, she saw how much work was needed below it before a safe welcome could begin.

chapterReports.title: 門邊的一盞燈
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The indoor model was nearly ready. Mira had used a small wheel and a little lamp to show how moving air could make light. The model did not get power from the old tower. It stood on a safe table in the village room, far from the closed door to the hill. Ben walked in with a ball under his arm and a piece of cheese in his lunch bag. "Can we show it tonight?" he asked. Mira said the class could see
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: was repaired. They understood the difference between a small teaching model and a full-size machine. Erin stepped back and watched. She did not need to be the person who spoke most loudly. The proof was on the table, in a simple model that worked and in children who could explain what they had seen. Tonight, the village room would be quiet again, but its next lesson was ready.

chapterReports.title: 一顆鬆弱的螺栓
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The repair team was close to finishing the work on the old tower. From the public bench, Ben could see a new piece of wood near the roof. He wanted to climb up for a better look, but Erin pointed down to the safe path. "You know why we stay here," she said. A baby in a nearby stroller laughed when a toy bat moved above her head. Her father sat on the bench with a plate of food. "We do not need to
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: bolt and do the full check again. Nobody tried to find a spare one somewhere just to make the deadline. Erin went home along the lower path, glad that the crew had found the problem before opening day. She thought of how often she had wanted the windmill to move. Now she wanted something more: to know that it could move safely, and to leave it still if that could not be shown.

chapterReports.title: 木頭上的名字
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The team replaced the bolt and began its tests. While the inspectors worked, Mr. Han came to the town office carrying a small pot with an old photograph inside a cloth bag. "Hello, Erin," he said. "I found this at the bottom of a drawer." The picture showed the first windmill builders and their families. One man had written his name on the back. Mr. Han explained that his wife had helped make the
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ised turning test. "So it is fine?" Ben asked. "It is fine for this step," she answered. "Not yet for visitors near the tower." Ben said yes and carefully changed the date on his drawing. Erin looked at the new display sign with its open space for more names. It was the kind of story she wanted to share: not one hero doing everything, but many people making room for each other.

chapterReports.title: 雨中的計畫變更
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The morning chosen for the first public visit was rainy. Erin heard the rain before she opened her eyes. Her cellphone showed a message from Nora: The outdoor visit must wait. The path needs a check after this storm. Erin sat up, disappointed but not surprised. She had invited friends from across the valley and hoped to meet them by the new bench. Now she needed to tell them that the outdoor part
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ried. Ms. Patel would decide whether the conditions were right for the final turning test. No one would promise a day until both checks were done. "We are close," Nora said. "I know," Erin answered. "And I do not want to lose what we have learned by hurrying at the end." Outside, the bell rang once through the wet air. Erin walked home with her notes held safely under her coat.

chapterReports.title: 風車轉動的早晨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: When the sky cleared, the repair team returned to the hill. They checked the new bolt, the brake, and the roof once more. The path team checked the ground, the drain, and the bench. Ms. Patel gave Nora a written safety notice after the tests. The tower itself would stay closed to visitors, but the lower path could open. On a day with the right wind, the trained team could make a short, supervised
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ch. Mr. Han rang the bell once more. "When you first came, you asked why the windmill stopped," he said. Erin nodded. "Now I know why it stopped, and why we were right not to hurry." Ben smiled. "And now we know how to take care of it." Erin looked at the hill, the safe path, and the people walking home. The story had found its ending, and the village had found a new beginning.

chapterReports.title: 沒有巴士的站牌
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At the north end of Dandelion Town, a red star was painted on an old wooden post. Nobody knew why the star was there. One morning, Koi, a young raccoon, saw a friendly woman standing beside it. The woman held a basket, a camera, and a little box for her pet bug. She wanted to reach the park for a family picnic, but her legs hurt when she walked far. The park was only on the other side of town. Sti
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: e down the child's wish to visit the park with his grandfather. Then she asked the father about work trips and the road to the farm. Every answer changed the map a little. At home, Koi put the paper on her desk. It was not a plan yet, only the beginning of one. She looked at the red star on her drawing and decided that an old empty post could become a place for a new beginning.

chapterReports.title: 池邊的桌子
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The next day, Koi asked anybody who used the town roads to come to a meeting. She borrowed the front room of an apartment near the old church. A clear window looked over the pond. There were only six chairs and one long sofa, so Dano brought two stools from his garage. Koi put a piece of paper and a pen on every seat. Some people came early. Others were late because the hill road was slow. “Here i
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: not look exciting, but it held the voices of her neighbors. Koi set it beside her bed and tried to sleep. She was not worried that people had different wishes. She was worried that she might forget one of them. Before turning out the light, she wrote a final line in dark ink: “Ask before deciding. Check before promising.” This time she did not need to guess what work came next.

chapterReports.title: 有兩個時鐘的道路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Koi and Dano began their road check near the school. A basketball rolled into the road, and three children ran after it. Dano stopped at once and waited until all the children were back behind the gate. “This area needs a slow speed,” he said. Koi wrote the fact in an email to the town hall. She wanted to define a safe stop as a place where people could wait away from moving vehicles. A stop besid
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: . “Will you help tell the other children where to wait?” He agreed and asked if he could draw a big picture for the wall. Koi said yes, as long as it showed the real waiting place. She saw that a plan was not only made by adults with tables and clocks. It could also grow when a child learned why a small choice kept everyone safe. She walked home with the new drawing in her bag.

chapterReports.title: 安靜的轉角
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the east side of town, a narrow street passed a green garden and a small bath house. Koi went there with Dano to check the road. They found a wooden bowl in the middle of the street. A family of ducks had been using it to feed a cute little dog. “The road is not a garden path,” Dano said gently. He moved the bowl back behind a fence, then looked both ways. The biggest problem was not the bowl.
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: hoice now. My grandson should not have to stand where he cannot see a car.” Koi sat with her for a moment. The light turned the garden leaves gold. “The new stop will not fix every trip,” Koi said, “but it can be a start.” Mrs. Pella smiled. For the first time that day, the old wall seemed less like an end to the road and more like a problem the town could work around together.

chapterReports.title: 月升時的農場路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first farm on the south road had many workers, but no one was sure where a bus could turn safely. Koi visited with Dano and a teenager named Elmo, who helped feed the hens. Elmo carried a yellow string and a small bottle of oil for the farm gate. “My father wants to sell fruit at the market,” he said. “The road looks straight on your map, but the ground is not.” Koi followed him through the fi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he red star on the map. “Remember the people who cannot walk to any of those places,” she said. Koi nodded. That was why the route had started. As she walked home, the moon followed her over the fields. She thought of the yellow string stretched beside the water channel. A good line was not just the shortest line; it was one that respected the people and the land on both sides.

chapterReports.title: 泥地上的座位
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: After two days of rain, the path to the shop was full of mud. Koi went to look at it with Nika, a mole who drew clear signs. At the roadside, a child was trying to pull a chair from a deep puddle. His arm was covered in brown water. “Do not step any farther,” Nika warned. She used a long stick to move the chair toward dry land, while Koi kept the child back. The little boy was surprised that a pla
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ieve more strongly that we must do it well.” Ressa reached for the back of the dry seat and sat down. From there she could see both the pond and the road. She said it was the first place on that street where she could rest without feeling in the way. Koi looked at the small seat and smiled. Even before the bus arrived, their questions had begun to make the town easier to cross.

chapterReports.title: 西花園的課
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Saturday, Nika held a class in a large garden on the west side of town. She wanted neighbors to learn how to read the new route map. A rabbit brought chocolate for the children, and a housewife named Mrs. Fira brought flowers for the table. Koi made a list of the places people wanted to visit. The main rule of the class was simple: nobody had to be good at reading maps to ask for help. One olde
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ,” she said. “That is not a big reason, but it is mine.” Koi made sure her wish was on the list. She had heard many requests for work, food, or health. She was glad to hear one about seeing a loved person. Dano closed the garden gate and said the real test of the route would be whether ordinary days became a little easier. Koi nodded. That was what the slow bus was meant to do.

chapterReports.title: 一個座位的價格
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At noon, Koi went to the town museum to look at old travel plans. A book on the shelf showed a train that once stopped outside Dandelion Town. The train had long gone, but its picture gave her an idea: a clear timetable could help people plan their day. The museum guide told her a story about a queen who traveled with more bags than people. Koi listened politely, then asked about real travel costs
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: that could be read in rain. Nika added a small amount for stronger cards. The final cost rose, but the plan became more honest. Koi put the three choices on the wall, with a clear note beside each one. She could not tell people what to choose. She could tell them what each choice meant. As the room emptied, Dano said he trusted a plan more when it showed its weak places openly.

chapterReports.title: 診所門前的歌
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Ressa wanted Koi to meet a bear named Odo who lived near the clinic. Odo had once been a singer, but he had stopped going out after his friend moved away. He felt lonely and sometimes sad. His house was warm, yet it was far from the market and the park. “A brave person is not someone who never needs help,” Ressa told him. Odo smiled at that. He invited Koi inside and showed her a photograph of a s
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: bus is a shared space, but each rider is still a person,” he said. Koi took the new map to Odo's home. He looked at the clinic stop and said it was close enough for him to walk. Then he asked if he could help make a quiet sound for the bus doors, so people with poor sight would know when they opened. Koi said they should test it with real passengers first. Odo was happy to try.

chapterReports.title: 傍晚測試
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Dano found a small bus that the town could borrow for one evening. It had a clear door and a button near the driver, but it did not yet have the signs for the new route. Dano had checked that his driving permit covered this vehicle. Koi walked around it slowly, checking the windows and steps. A student from the school came to watch, carrying a menu from his mother's food stand. He had been helping
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: had returned without anyone getting hurt. She wrote the true time beside each stop and added a wide space for notes. She also drew a small rose by the narrow corner so she would remember it. She did not want the next test to be perfect in a story. She wanted it to be safer in real life. On her desk, the first red-star map was growing into something more careful and more useful.

chapterReports.title: 醫院前的白線
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Koi returned to the hospital with Nika and a basket of drawing tools. They came to check the new waiting area. A nurse asked them to mark a white line well away from the emergency door. “Dear friends,” she said, smiling, “please do not make the door hard to reach.” Nika checked the color of the paint against the gray road. It was clear in the sun, but hard to see under a shadow. They tried a diffe
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: busy day, when the hospital was full. Koi agreed to return during visiting hours. She pinned the latest picture beside her first map and could see how much had changed. The small white line on the road looked ordinary. To Koi, it held many conversations and careful choices. A good stop was not one good idea. It was many small, useful ideas tested by the people who needed them.

chapterReports.title: 四點鐘的車票
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At four o’clock in the afternoon, the town hall held a small open meeting. An actor from the local theater came with a band of young musicians. They wanted to celebrate the first bus test with a song, but Koi explained that this was not the last test. They still needed a safe route and a fair ticket plan. One musician, who wore round glasses, asked whether they could play at the bus stop. “You can
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ople could see the number clearly, but one picture looked too much like a package label. Nika promised to change it. Koi took all the notes home. She knew people wanted the bus to begin, and she did too. Still, she could not hurry through rules that would affect someone's daily life. She marked the next meeting on her calendar, then went to sleep with her shoes beside the door.

chapterReports.title: 果園上方的路
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: A beautiful brown duck named Poma invited Koi to a small camp area above the orchard. She said a group of young hikers wanted to ride the bus to the high field on weekends. Koi went with Dano and two members of the walking club. The path was wide near the bottom, but turned into a narrow stair beside a hill. A bus could not climb those steps. Some hikers began to fight over where the route should
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: me passengers needed a clinic door. Others wanted the start of a walk. A route could serve both, as long as people knew where the bus ended and where their own path began. She drew a clear end mark on the map. Poma looked at it and said she would explain the choice to her club. Koi thanked her. They had not won every argument, but they had made a plan everyone could understand.

chapterReports.title: 誠實的延誤
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Koi arrived at the town hall carrying a bag of new signs. Nika had packed several sizes of letters, a bottle of water, and a small drawing of an ant to remind children to stand in a line. At the door, a chicken clerk told them that the road approval would take longer than expected. A paper had gone to the wrong room. Koi was upset, but she did not blame the clerk for a mistake he had just found. “
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ew road line had been checked. “That is real work too,” she said. Koi looked at the large notices on the table. She had planned to finish signs and maps, but had spent the day correcting information instead. It was not the work she wanted, yet people needed it. She opened her book and wrote, “An honest delay is better than a false start.” Then she prepared for the next morning.

chapterReports.title: 早班路線上的禮物
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On a bright morning, Koi found a lovely gift outside the town hall: a small box with pencils and a note of thanks. It came from a daughter whose father wanted to visit the tennis court again. He had stopped going because the walk was too long. The note said that he hoped the new route would give him a chance to watch his friends play. Koi put the note in her pocket. It was a pleasure to see that p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: d soon be able to go every day. She explained the trial and showed the proposed stop. He said one morning each week would already make a great difference. Koi listened carefully. What looked like a small service on a timetable could become a lovely part of someone else's life. She went home more certain of what the first bus was meant to protect: choice, time, and ordinary joy.

chapterReports.title: 每位乘客的一頁
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Nika brought a stack of bright paper to Koi's desk. She had drawn a new map with clear pictures, but one page was gray and hard to read. “We must change this one,” she said. Koi agreed. They made a habit of asking people to test signs before printing many copies. An older pig named Bemi came to help. He could read very small letters, but his grandfather could not. Bemi said they should hold each p
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: began to ride. Bemi helped her sort the papers into two boxes, one for the stops and one for the bus. Dano checked the boxes against the list and locked the room. On the walk home, Koi thought about the grandfather holding the rail and the visitor asking about the star. Both had helped make one simple map better. The work was very ordinary, and that was exactly why it mattered.

chapterReports.title: 圓圈測試
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Monday, Dano drove the empty bus to a wide yard beside the market. Koi and Nika had built a circle of light wooden cones to mark the turning space. They wanted to test whether the bus could turn without touching anything. A young friend named Etti brought a drum and wanted to beat it when the bus passed. Dano asked her to wait, because he needed to hear the engine and the voices of people guidi
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: down what most of the team had learned: a safe turn took space, a safe test took permission, and a safe road had room for living trees. She also wrote what she herself wanted to remember. People had helped not because they all liked the same things, but because they wanted their town to work better. She felt lucky to have friends who could tell her when a plan needed to change.

chapterReports.title: 巴士上的十二個位置
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The borrowed bus had room for a dozen passengers, and today the team would check every seat. Dano parked it along the hall wall. He brought bread for lunch, but he did not let anyone eat while the safety test was under way. Koi carried a ruler and a roll of tape. She wanted to mark the distance between the door and the first seat, then check whether people could move through the aisle. A young vis
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: tched Ressa use the entrance. She got on slowly, but comfortably. Dano waited until she was fully seated before moving his hand from the door. No one drove the bus that morning. Still, Koi wrote down an important result: the entrance could be used safely in a parked test. She had wanted a perfect day. Instead she had learned that taking a step back could move a project forward.

chapterReports.title: 第一次練習搭乘
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The council gave permission for a practice ride with a small group of invited volunteers. No fares would be collected, and the bus would travel only on the approved roads. Koi stood beside Dano and checked the list on her computer. She felt cool morning air through the open door. A mother arrived with her son, carrying a cup of water and a bag of food. She wanted to show him how to sit safely. A l
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: oling beside her. The practice had not been perfect. They had found a storage problem and a sign that needed to be moved. But every volunteer had reached the correct stop safely. Koi wrote “first ride completed” in her book and drew a small square around the words. She was proud, not because the bus had become famous, but because it had done the simple job they had asked of it.

chapterReports.title: 環線上的雨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the morning of the final road test, dark clouds began to appear over the mountain. An elephant named Ravo had come to town with a violin, hoping to travel with the first bus group. Koi explained that the test had room only for the named volunteers. Ravo was disappointed, but he did not argue. He went to wait at the community hall. Dano looked at the sky and said they might have to stop the test
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: he first day. The promise she had made was not that the bus would always run, no matter what. She had promised to find a safe way for people to travel. Rain had not broken that promise. It had shown why the promise mattered. Koi wiped the edge of the map board and checked that the new notice was easy to read. Then she walked home as the clouds moved slowly away from the valley.

chapterReports.title: 關於明天的會議
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the first Monday of the month, the town council held a meeting about the slow bus. Koi brought a map, a cost report, and a clear list of the work still needed. Dano sat near the door. A young mouse from the garden club came with his mother and a guitar, but he left the instrument in its case so the meeting would be quiet. The mayor said the service might begin with a short trial after the next
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ested on a bench. The town was still full of ordinary sounds: carts, birds, footsteps, and voices from the market. Koi looked toward the north road and thought of the empty post. It had taken more than a month to reach this moment, and there were still things to check. But a place that once meant waiting for nothing might soon become a place where someone could begin a journey.

chapterReports.title: 工程師的最後檢查
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The final vehicle check began early. An engineer named Salo came with a small glass light and a thick book of rules. He looked at the bus floor, the door, the handrail, and the seats. Koi watched carefully but did not tell him how to do his work. Nika had drawn pictures showing where people should sit and where bags belonged. Salo checked whether the drawings matched the real space. The bus was on
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: morrow, if the wet road was clear, the first public ride could begin. Koi felt hungry and tired, but she was not sorry about the extra check. The simple thing she wanted was for people to go from one place to another and return home safely. She tucked the report into a dry folder and carried it to the town hall. There, it would be kept with the records anyone could ask to read.

chapterReports.title: 路上的記號
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On the morning before the first public ride, Koi went to check the signs. She found a big red mark on the ground near the west stop. At first she thought someone had made a piece of art. Then Nika showed her a thick branch hanging over the path. The mark was a warning from a gardener. He had expected workers to cut the branch, but no one had come yet. Koi did not step under it. She put up a tempor
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: of people going home. She ran her hand over the new sign and looked at the red mark, which was still faintly visible on the ground. She did not erase it yet. It reminded her that even on the last day of preparation, a plan could need another careful look. She was glad the town had taken time to act. Tomorrow's trip would mean more because the way to the bus had been made safe.

chapterReports.title: 第一個公開載客早晨
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first public bus began on a warm morning after the road workers gave their final approval. Koi went to the north stop early. She was almost too excited to eat the carrot bread she had bought for breakfast. Ressa arrived in a light jacket, walking carefully with her stick. She looked glad to see that the old red-star post now had a clear timetable beside it. A small insect sat on the edge of th
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: was why the trial would last a month. Koi put the first-day report in the public folder and wrote down the next review date. She did not call the project finished. It was now part of people's days, and that meant they had to keep listening. Dano looked tired but pleased. “We did not build a fast bus,” he said. “We made a way for more people to choose where they go.” Koi agreed.

chapterReports.title: 留下來的站牌
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: Four weeks later, the council met again. Koi was able to show a full month of records: safe trips, a few late arrivals, and changes people wanted. She had been afraid the bus would have to say goodbye after the trial. Instead, the council agreed to allow the slow bus to continue for another season, with a clear review date. The service was not perfect, but it was comfortable for most riders and ha
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: as waiting there. Koi smiled. A good driver followed the route, not every friendly wave. She turned toward home, then looked back once. The empty post had not been taken away. It had become a real place in the town. Tomorrow there would be work, new questions, and perhaps another change. For tonight, she could simply be glad that the slow bus belonged to everyone who needed it.

chapterReports.title: 給星星的教室
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: At 7 a.m., Nia stood outside her apartment on Red Brick Street, her heavy teaching bag resting beside the breakfast table. She was early for her first class and had plenty of time to prepare. The city center had given her a room for six Saturday lessons about the night sky. Nia loved stars, but she had never taught a class alone. Before leaving, she sat down to finish her breakfast. There was frui
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: ere only dots from a lamp, but they made the room feel different. Finn returned with his mother and gasped when he saw them. "Can we make more?" he asked. "Yes," Nia replied, "after we learn how to work safely." She had hoped for a full room on the first day. For now, a grandmother, a cook, and one curious child were enough to begin. She turned off the lamp and locked the door.

chapterReports.title: 六週計畫
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Monday, Nia met the center director, Mr. Hale, to learn the rules. The center could offer the room for six weeks, but it had only a small amount of money for paper and lamps. After six weeks, the city would read the class notes and decide whether the lessons could continue. Nia asked if numbers alone would matter. "No," Mr. Hale said. "We need to know who can take part and what they learn." Her
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: activity and one question to take home. Ada took a photo of the notice to share with the library. "It may not sound exciting," she said. Nia read it again and smiled. "It sounds honest." The two women put the notice at eye level, not too high. People walking past the center could read it without stopping in the street. That was the first part of their plan that was truly ready.

chapterReports.title: 從道路望出去
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: The first Saturday began with a walk, not a telescope. Nia wanted everyone to know where the sun went down and why the sky looked different from one place to another. Eight people came, including Finn, Mrs. Sol, and a boy named Bo. They followed a clean path from the center toward the beach. The route crossed a small bridge, then turned beside a bus station. Nia asked the group to stand on the saf
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: er slow down. Bo said that he liked the bird, but he did not like waiting beside the road. Ada wrote both comments beside the map. These notes were not a test of the people. They were a test of the lesson. Nia moved the next week's outdoor plan to a shorter path. She also made a rule: any person could ask for a break. Looking at the sky should never mean leaving someone behind.

chapterReports.title: 牆上的小雲
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: On Tuesday, a strong wind began to blow through Red Brick Street. A dark cloud covered the sun. Nia watched a butterfly fly past the window and wondered how she could explain the weather in simple words. Downstairs, a worker from the paper factory had come to fix a door. He saw her blue paper squares and said they looked like little pieces of the sky. "That is the idea," Nia said. "We want to make
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: dow, turn the fan off, and move the chairs away from the stairs. These small jobs took time. Nia used to think that a teacher's work began when the children arrived. Now she saw that a good lesson also needed quiet work before and after. She left the room with the weather report in her hand and a new question in her mind: Could a cloudy day still be a good day for a star class?

chapterReports.title: 星星有多高
chapterReports.sceneOpeningEn: For the next lesson, Nia made a long paper ruler. Finn wanted to know the height of a star, but she explained that stars were too far away to measure with an ordinary ruler. "Then what is the point of this?" he asked. Nia showed how the ruler could help them compare the height of a lamp and a picture on the wall. That was something they could truly measure. During the lesson, Mrs. Sol put a small
chapterReports.sceneClosingEn: . Mrs. Sol said she liked the chair path and the new large numbers. Nia looked at the room. It was not full, but it had become a place where people made changes together. She did not know if the city would let them stay after six weeks. For now, she put the two rulers, one wet and one dry, into a box. They would remind her that a lesson could grow from a question and a mistake.

chapterReports.title: 盒子裡的月亮
